PROPER UTILISATION OF FUNDS
Recommendation/Observation
5. The statement showing the amount allocated and expenditure incurred under various schemes of the
Ministry of Culture shows that the total funds allocated to various schemes of the Ministry has increased
from 
` 236.07 crores in Financial Year (FY) 2016-17 to ` 318.73 crores in FY 2018-19, which is an increase
of about 35%. Yet, the amount allocated to the “Scheme for Safeguarding the Intangible Cultural Heritage
and Diverse Cultural Traditions of India” remains stagnant at ` 3.50 crores and has not seen a commensurate
increase. Moreover , even out of the paltry ` 3.50 crores allocated to this Scheme, the Ministry was able to
spend only ` 0.65 crores in the FY 2016-17. This points to a huge gap between the on-paper plans of the
Ministry for this Scheme and its execution thereof. In this regard, the Committee desires that the Ministry of
Culture should analyze the reasons for under utilization of funds for this scheme. The Committee is of the
view that the damage dealt to intangible Cultural heritage is irreparable and hence, the Ministry should
ensure proper utilization of funds for the implementation of this scheme. (Para 26 & 27)
Reply of the Ministry
5.1 The Scheme for Safeguarding the Intangible Cultural Heritage and Diverse Cultural Traditions of India
was formulated in the year 2013 to support and strengthen the efforts of various stakeholders vis-à-vis
wider recognition and acceptance, dissemination, preservation and promotion of the rich, diverse and vast
Intangible Cultural Heritage of India.
5.2 Under the scheme, there is an Expert Committee comprising of eminent ICH experts, formed to
scrutinize/ screen the proposals/ applications. However, the tenure of the Expert Committee was constituted
for a tenure of two years expired in 2016 and could not be reconstituted for a long time which led to the
under utilisation of funds allocated for the same.
5.3 However, now the Expert Committee has been reconstituted and it is expected that the scheme would
now be implemented more smoothly.
Further Recommendation/Observation:
5.4 The Committee is at a loss to understand as to why there was such a long delay in reconstituting
the Expert Committee (EC) when an allocation of ````` 3.50 crores was made for the Financial Year
2017-18. It is really intriguing as to how the EC responsible for an important scheme like this could
be allowed to be non-functional for such a long period. The Committee feels that since the tenure of
the EC is known beforehand, the requisite actions to reconstitute the EC should have been set in
motion well before the tenure of the EC expired in 2016. The Committee may be apprised of the
reasons for the undue delay in reconstitution of the Expert Committee. The Committee may also

12
be updated on the financial performance under the head ‘Scheme for Safeguarding the Intangible
Cultural Heritage and Diverse Cultural Traditions of India’ in FY 2019-20.
Recommendation/Observation
6. The Committee observes a pattern of underutilisation of funds for the “Scheme of Financial Assistance
for Creation of Cultural Infrastructure” in Financial Years 2016-17 and 2017-18. The Committee recommends
that Ministry should look into the matter and come up with ways and means to properly utilize the allocated
funds for this Scheme. (Para 28)
Reply of the Ministry
6.1 The components of the scheme for Financial Assistance for Creation of Cultural Infrastructure are
Building Grant and Tagore Cultural Complexes. As and when proposal complete in all aspects comes from
different states of India, the proposal was examined in accordance with the guidelines and eligible proposals
referred to the expert committee for consideration. The Ministry is utilizing allocated funds for the respective
schemes in a transparent way.
Further Recommendation/Observation:
6.2 The Committee is constrained to note that the reply of the Ministry is vague and devoid of any
relevant facts. While disapproving the Ministry’s half-hearted approach in implementing the Scheme
for Financial Assistance for Creation of Cultural Infrastructure in FY 2016-17 and 2017-18, the
Committee observes that had the Ministry effectively taken up the matter with the State
Governments for timely finalization of their proposals, funds allocated under this head would not
have remained unutilized. Non-drawal of funds not only reflects poorly on the functioning of the
Ministry but also impacts on creation of Cultural Infrastructure in the country. The Committee
desires to be kept updated on the financial performance under the above head.
Recommendation/Observation
7. The Committee notes that the “Scheme for Promotion of Culture of Science” in Financial Year 2017-
18 could only utilize 
` 32.60 crores out of the ` 39.00 crores that were allocated to the Ministry. Given the

Haryana and Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh and upgradation Regional Science Centre, Dehradun to a Science City.

the age group of 10 to 14 years and 18 to 25 years both respectively, the details of which are as follows:-
8.1.1  Cultural Talent Search Scholarship Scheme :
The Cultural Talent Search Scholarship Scheme aims at providing facilities to selected meritorious
young children to develop their talents in various performing, visual & literary art fields. Children
in the age group of 10 to 14 years studying either in recognized schools or belonging to families
practicing traditional arts forms are selected for the scholarships. The scholarship awarded
under the Scheme is initially for two years and is renewable after every two years till the
completion of the first University degree stage of education or upto the age of 20 years, whichever
is earlier subject to the awardee maintaining satisfactory progress.
8.1.2  Scheme of “Award of Scholarships to Young Artistes (SYA) in different Cultural fields”:
The Scheme for “Award of Scholarships to Young Artistes (SYA) in different Cultural fields”
have also been transferred to CCRT partially under which 400 scholarships are provided in the

14
age group of 18 to 25 years in the field of Indian Classical Music, Classical Dances, Light
Classical Music, Theatre, Visual Arts and Folk/ Traditional and Indigenous Arts. The panel
related to various arts forms are constituted by the Ministry of Culture, Govt. of India.
8.1.3  Scheme for the “Award of Junior and Senior Fellowship” in the field of Culture :
The Ministry of Culture, Govt. of India transferred its scheme titled “The Scheme for the Award
of Fellowship to Outstanding Persons in the Field of Culture” in the year 2014 to CCRT. The
focus of this scheme is on “in- depth study/research” in various facets of culture. These include
new emerging areas of Cultural Studies. The broad area of research are mainly on the field of
Classical Music, Light Classical Music, Dance and Dance Music, Folk/Traditional and indigenous
Art, Literature, New Areas, Theatre and Visual Art.
8.2 Following actions are being taken to ensure that no scam occurs in the future:-
8.2.1 Transparency in the allocation of funds: Utmost efforts are made for allocation of funds as
funds are transferred through RTGS/NEFT/PFMS.
8.2.2 Proper utilization of funds: The funds are utilized with maximum transparency and reach to the
beneficiaries as transferred through RTGS/NEFT/PFMS. Proper and duly signed payment receipts
are received from Guru & Parents etc.
Further Recommendation/Observation:
8.3 The Committee notes the steps taken by the Ministry to ensure that such frauds do not take
place in future, but the Ministry has been found lacking in its efforts. The Committee reiterates
that software solutions must be developed to detect and curb the possibility of any such incidents
and the employees involved in the disbursement of the scheme funds should be well trained on it.
The Committee would like to know the actual process being followed to obtain duly signed payment
receipts from Guru, Parents etc. and steps taken to prevent scams which deprive the deserving
recipients of the fellowships and schemes.

I Brief Background 
 The tourism sector has huge potential as an instrument for economic 
development.  Tourism is also an important source of foreign exchange earnings.  Not 
only does the tourism sector spearhead growth, it also improves the quality of people‟s 
lives with its capacity to create large -scale employment of diverse kind.  It also 
supports environmental protection and champions diverse cultural heritage.  
2.  Ministry of Tourism is the nodal agency to formulate national  policies  and  
programmes for the development an d promotion of tourism. In the process, the 
Ministry consults and collaborates with other stakeholders in the sector including 
various Central Ministries/ Agencies, State Governments/ Union Territory 
Administrations and the representatives of the private sector. 
3. Secretary (Tourism) is the executive chief of the Ministry. The Directorate 
General of Tourism has 20 Domestic field offices and an Indian Institute of Skiing and 
Mountaineering within the country and 08 overseas offices. The overseas offices 
promote Indian tourism in the markets abroad. 
4. The domestic field offices also play a vital role for promotion of tourism sector 
in the country. They are also involved in monitoring the progress of implementation of 
projects sanctioned by the Ministry to the Stat e Governments/Union Territories. India 
Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC) is the only public sector undertaking under 
the charge of the Ministry of Tourism.  
5. The Ministry also has the following autonomous institutions: 
(i) Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management (IITTM). 
(ii) National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology 
(NCHMCT); and the Institutes of Hotel Management (IHMs). 
(iii) Indian Culinary Institute (ICI). 
Role and Functions of the Ministry of Tourism 
5.1. The Ministry has the following main functions: 
i) All policy matters including:   
a. Development Policies 
b. Incentives 
c. External Assistance 
d. Manpower Development 
e. Promotion & Marketing 
f. Investment Facilitation 
g. Growth Strategies 
ii) Planning 
iii) Co -ordination with other Ministries, Departments, States/Union Territory 
Administrations. 
iv) Regulation: 
a. Standards 
b. Guidelines

a. Central Assistance 
b. Distribution of Tourism Products 
vi) Research, Analysis, Monitoring and Evaluation 
vii) International Co-operation and External Assistance: 
a. International Bodies 
b. Bilateral Agreements 
c. External Assistance 
d. Foreign Technical Collaboration 
viii)  Legislation and Parliamentary Work 
ix)  Establishment Matters 
x) Overall Review of the Functioning of the Field Offices 
xi) Vigilance Matters 
xii) Official Language: Implementation of Official Language Policy 
xiii) VIP References 
xiv) Budget Co-ordination and Related Matters 
xv) Plan Co-ordination 
xvi) Overseas Marketing (OM) Work 
xvii) Welfare, Grievances and Protocol

23. The Committee notes that due to broad budgetary cuts imposed by the 
Ministry of Finance, the Ministry has witnessed a reduction in allocation of funds 
for the financial year 2020 -21 and has been allocated only Rs. 2499.83 crore as 
against its projected demand of Rs. 2647.25 crore. 
24. The Committee also notes that less allocation as compared to the projecte d 
demand is not unique to the financial year 2020 -21.  Against the projected 
demands of Rs. 4320.42 Crore and Rs. 4612.18 Crore for Financial Year 2018 -19 
and 2019-20 respectively, Ministry of Finance provided Rs. 2150.00 crore and Rs. 
2189.22 crore in BE 2018-19 and BE 2019 -20 respectively which were further

25. The Committee observes that tourism being a labour -intensive multi -
sectoral activity characteri sed by multiple services and industries is a key driver 
of socio -economic progress as well as employment generation and economic 
development.  The tourism sector has the potential to stimulate other economic 
sectors through its backward and forward linkage s and cross -sectoral synergies 
with sectors like agriculture, handicrafts, transport, construction, to name a few.  
It is thus evident that any higher investment made in the tourism sector can lead 
to large sale employment generation, alleviate poverty and  propel India to a 
faster growth trajectory.   
26. The Committee is dismayed to note that despite its unique endowments of 
biodiversity and its rich culture and heritage, India‘s total share in global 
international tourist arrivals remains a modest 1.24% a gainst the target of 3% 
while, as per the Report of the Working Group of Tourism of the 12 th Five Year 
Plan, in about 150 countries of the world, tourism is one of the 5 top export 
earners and number one export earner in about 60 countries. When measured by 
the yardstick of its vast tourism resources, India‘s low share of tourism arrivals 
is certainly below its potential.  Similarly, the contribution (direct and indirect) 
of tourism in the GDP and the total jobs in the country is estimated to be 5.06% 
and 12.75% respectively, which, in the considered opinion of the Committee, is 
inadequate and way  below the massive potential that exists. The Committee 
wishes to point out that in many smaller and developing countries , the entire 
economy of the country depends on tourism for its survival and tourism remains 
a major source of foreign exchange earnings . That being the case , the world's 
second largest country in terms of population, seventh largest by area, having 
7500 km of coastline and one of the most endowed regions of the world in terms 
of its tourism attractiveness, India receives less internationa l tourists than its full 
potential.  Taking all these factors into account, the Committee apprehends that 
the shortfall of Rs. 147.42 crore in BE 2020 -21 against the projected demand of 
Rs. 2647.25 crore would seriously jeopardize the targeted tourism outc omes 
during the Financial Year 2020-21.  

 
 
14 
 
27.    The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that the difference in 
the projection made by it and the allocation given for the financial year 2020 -21 
is not high and that if additional funds are require d, it would move the Ministry 
of Finance for additional allocation at the RE 2020 -21 stage.  The Committee 
observes that availability of adequate resources to the tourism sector is sine qua 
non for achieving the tourism growth as well as inclusive growth.  Since 
development of tourism infrastructure is capital intensive, the Committee 
apprehends that with the budgetary allocation of Rs.2499.83 crore for 2020 -21, 
which, in the opinion of the Committee, is low, it would be difficult for the 
Ministry to take u p significant activities related to on -going infrastructure 
development of the sanctioned tourism circuits/destinations and also 
development of new tourism products of global standards.  If the tourism sector 
has to play a major role in faster and inclusiv e growth, the infrastructure 
bottlenecks need to be unleashed.  The Committee notes that more than half of 
the allocation of the Ministry for 2020 -21 is devoted for the schemes relating to 
infrastructure development.  In most of the States/UTs, the outlay for tourism is 
meagre and the Central Government has dominance in the domain of public 
resource mobilization by w ay of collection of tax revenue.  The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry be provided a higher financial outlay at the RE 
2020-21 stage.  The  Committee would like the Ministry of Tourism to bring the 
above recommendation to the notice of Ministry of Finance and also intimate the 
Committee of their response in this regard.    
28.    Since the consumption demand arising from tourist expenditure h as a 
multiplier effect on the economy, the expansion of the tourist sector can lead to 
large scale employment gene ration and poverty alleviation. Needless to mention, 
tourism has huge potential to stimulate overall economic growth and any 
increase in the o utlay for tourism sector can propel our country to a faster 
growth trajectory and will lead to large scale employment generation and 
alleviation of poverty. If our country can tap its full potential of the tourism 
sector, it can play a major role for faste r and inclusive growth;  but for this to 
happen, the budgetary provisions for the Ministry has to be enhanced 

 
 
15 
 
substantially.  By doing so, tourism infrastructure could be strengthened/ 
upgraded, conservation and development of all heritage sites could be 
undertaken and completed and last mile connectivity to tourist de stinations could 
be improved. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government 
should accord priority status to the tourism sector and enumerate a fiscal 
roadmap for generating and allo cating more financial resource for tourism so 
that the full potential of a vibrant sector could be tapped. 
29. The Committee notes with dismay the huge mismatch between the 
projected demand for funds and actual allocations made for the Ministry of 
Tourism for the years 2018 -19 and 2019 -20 as well.  The pattern of shortfall in 
allocation of funds indicates that budgetary requirements are being projected by 
the Ministry more on the basis of theoretical anticipation rather than on actual 
trend of requirement. The Ministry‘s reply that the Schemes/Projects 
undertaken by them are of continuous nature and that the targets are fixed and 
funds are released as per budgetary allocation by the Ministry of Finance 
suggests the casual and routine manner in which the Budg et Estimates are being 
prepared and the Ministry is not very serious about the activities to be 
undertaken by them.  Tourism is important for both economic growth and 
employment generation and the corpus of funds should not have been arbitrarily 
decided without reference to any ground reality.   
30. The Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to have the entire 
requirement of funds realistically assessed after collecting timely information on 
requirement of funds from the State Governments and other s takeholders and 
take steps to rectify and improve upon the existing system of assessing 
requirement of funds. The Ministry should formulate Schemes/Programmes 
which can be implemented in a time -bound manner.  The Committee desires to 
be apprised of the specific action taken in this regard. 
31. The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the Ministry has kept the 
unspent provisions of Rs. 43.18 Crore till the close of the financial year 2018 -19 
and surrendered the same on 29.03.2019 totally disregardin g the provisions of 

 
 
16 
 
General Financial Rules which states that unspent provisions in a grant should  
be surrendered as soon as they  are foreseen, without waiting for the last day of 
the year.  The Committee deprecates such a casual approach of the Ministry in 
adhering to the fiscal discipline and desires the Ministry to avoid such lapses in 
future and surrender unspent budgetary provisions timely s o that starved 
projects/schemes are not deprived of the same. 
32. The Committee takes note of the fact that the annual growth rate of the 
Tourism Sector in India is 5.2% and its contribution to GDP is 5.06%. According 
to UN World Tourism Organisation Report (2011), for diversified economies, the 
contribution of tourism to national GDP is over 10% for countries where tourism 
happens to be the main driver of national economy. Quite apparently, despite 
having a strong domestic tourist base which is likely  to grow further on the back 
of a rapidly rising middle class with increased disposable incomes and having 
many World Heritage sites and rich fauna, our country has not been able to 
exploit its tourism potential to the fullest possible extent and the touri st sector 
has not proved to be the proverbial engine of growth for our economy. For a 
country of our size, with wealth of attractions and experiences, this 
underperformance represents significant foregone economic value. Since tourism 
in the country has th e potential to emerge as a key economic driver through 
economic growth and employment generation, the country can make a giant leap 
towards achieving 5 trillion dollar economy by tapping the enormous potential of 
the tourism sector. The Committee, therefor e, recommends that the strategies 
adopted for promotion and development of the tourist sector should be 
recalibrated to harness the full potential of Indian tourism and double the 
current contribution of tourism to GDP in the next 5 years. The Committee 
would like the Ministry to prepare a vision document, chalking out a road map 
for accelerating the expansion of the tourism sector and helping achieve a 5 
trillion dollar economy by 2025 by way of a substantial contribution from the 
tourism sector. The Commi ttee, therefore, desires that policy measures may be 
initiated by the Ministry to accelerate the growth momentum of the tourism 

 
 
17 
 
sector and raise the contribution of tourism from the current 5.06% to 10% of 
GDP. 
33. The Committee notes from the information made available to it , that a 
substantial amount of Rs. 245.308 crore is involved in pending Utilization 
Certificates (UCs) under various Schemes/ Programmes of the Ministry.  Since 
conditionality regarding submission of UCs is an absolute bar for release o f 
funds, the Committee apprehends that the pendency of UCs may impinge on the 
implementation of the flagship Schemes/Projects of the Ministry.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should put in place a 
dedicated mechanism to ensure that all pending UCs are liquidated within a 
period of six months from the presentation of this Report. 
III Integrated Development of Tourist Circuits Around Specific Themes 
(Swadesh Darshan) 
 
34. The Union Government, in the Union Budget 2014 -15, decided to cr eate tourist 
circuits around specific themes.  The Swadesh Darshan Scheme was, therefore, launched

56. The Committee is constrained  to observe that under the Swadesh Darshan 
Scheme (SDS), out of the 77 projects sanctioned so far for Rs. 6035.70 Crore, 
only 9 Projects have reached their logical conclusion and the remaining projects 
have witnessed physical progress ranging from 50% to 90% and 10 projects have 
not even  taken off due to non -release of funds. The Committee also notes that no 
new projects have been sanctioned during 2019 -20, though the Ministry has not 
adduced any reasons for this.  The Committe e further notes with serious concern 
that against the sanctioned provision of Rs. 6035.70 Crore under the SDS, only 
Rs. 3744.00 crore have so far been released.  It is a matter of anguish for the 
Committee that such substantial variations have occurred bet ween the 
sanctioned provisions and the actual release and expenditure.  Obviously, these 
instances betray absence of a sound budgetary mechanism for assessing the 

 
 
25 
 
actual requirements of funds.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry should address this issue squarely and devise a foolproof mechanism to 
overcome the deficiencies in the existing system of assessing the requirement of 
funds under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme. 
57. The Committee takes note of the remedial measures formulated by the  
Ministry for effective implementation of the projects sanctioned under the SDS 
and would like the Ministry to carry out an appraisal of their efficacy so that the 
avowed objective of developing world class infrastructure in the circuit 
destinations, promoting cultural and heritage value of the country and providing 
complete tourism experience with varied thematic circuits under the Scheme 
could be achieved. 
58. The Committee is of the view that though the Ministry reviews the 
progress of the projects const antly under the SDS, the absence of a dedicated 
monitoring mechanism at the State level is hampering the performance and goals 
of the projects sanctioned under it.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry should , without further loss of time , take up the issue with the 
concerned State Governments at the highest level to understand their constraints 
in implementation of tourism projects and put in place a dedicated mechanism 
for implementation of the projects as it has a direct bearing on the timelines set 
for these projects.  Such a focused monitoring would go a long way in speeding 
up long pending SDS projects crucial for enhancing the tourist attractiveness and 
realising the tourism potential of India‘s assets. 
59. The Committee observes that rural tourism is among a few emerging areas 
of tourist interest world -wide.  Rural tourism is important because it helps in 
inclusive development of remote and backward areas by way of enhancing 
earning capacity and better livel ihood for the rural population.  As of now, two 
projects with a sanctioned outlay of Rs. 125.02 crore have been approved under 
Rural Circuit out of which only Rs. 21.24 Crore has been released for a project in 
Bihar while no funds have been released for an other sanctioned Rural Circuit in 
Kerala which is indicative of the snail‘s pace of progress in the matter.  The 

 
 
26 
 
Committee is of the opinion that had the Ministry made co -ordinated efforts with 
the State Government of Kerala , the handicaps in implementing the project 
could have been ironed out and the project could have kick started. 
60. The Committee recommends that for better promotion of rural  tourism, a 
cluster approach may be pursued rather than a stand -alone approach and more 
and more Rural Circuit P rojects may be sanctioned and implemented for 
promotion of niche tourism and more funds may be earmarked for rural circuits 
under the SDS. 
61. The Committee is dismayed to note that all 5 Buddhist Circuit Projects 
costing Rs. 355.26 Crore have witnessed ti me overruns.  The reasons attributed 
by the Ministry  include land availability, delay in statutory clearances, delay in 
tendering work by implementing agencies, etc.  The Committee is of the firm 
view that had the Ministry completed pre -project activities  including clearance 
before sanction of these projects or before award of contract, persistent problem 
of time overrun could have been easily avoided.  Now that the Ministry has 
revised the guidelines of the scheme in 2017, the Committee expects that the 
sanctioned Buddhist Circuit Projects would be implemented expeditiously and 
the issues related to time overrun would be resolved.  The Committee desires to 
be apprised of the outcome in this regard. 
62. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should  pursue with all 
the State Governments the matter of setting up of a State Level Monitoring 
Committee to remove various impediments like delays in land acquisition and 
statutory clearances so that time overrun in Buddhist Circuit Projects is 
minimized.  Th is would also speed up execution of Buddhist Circuit Projects 
within the approved cost.

execution of the project is decent.  Phy sical progress is more than 40% and 
the state government is committed to complete the project by Sept. 2020.

clearances, which took considerable long time.  The project was reviewed by

75. The Committee notes that the PRASHAD has been launched  with the 
objective of holistic development of identified pilgrimage and heritage 
destinations and aims at infrastructure development.  Since the provision of 
infrastructure is a prerequisite towards improving the country‘s tourism 
productive capacity and attracting more tourists, the delay being witnessed in the 
expeditious operationalization of PRASHAD projects is pathetic and is suggestive 
of laxity in the monitoring system of the Ministry and the State Governments. 
This leaves the Committee wondering as  to how the Ministry would achieve their 

 
 
35 
 
envisaged objective of this Scheme.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that 
the shortcoming noticed in implementation of the projects under the PRASHAD 
should be addressed quickly. The Committee also recommends that the projects 
initiated under the PRASHAD should have a definite date of completion. Unless 
this is done, ambitious budgeting without commensurate capacity to deliver the 
desired outcomes under the PRASHAD would remain a futile exercise. The 
Committee also recommends that the achievements of the targets set under 
PRASHAD be analysed in detail for formulating remedial measures.  
76. The Committee is constrained to note nil progress in respect of four 
PRASHAD Project s, namely, (i) Development of Omkareshwar,  (ii) Cruise 
tourism in river Ganga (Varanasi), (iii) Development of Varanasi II and (iv) 
Development of Trimbakeshwar (Nasik) during the year 2017 -18. The 
Committee is further constrained to note that the reasons behind the lack of 
progress in implementing them were the deficiencies in project formulation and 
delay in obtaining all required clearances.  It is obvious that the efforts of the 
Ministry towards operationalization of the above projects have been undertaken 
in a piecemeal manner.  Though the Ministry has informed the Committee that 
appropriate corrective measures have been taken to eradicate t he deficiencies in 
project formulation and obtain all necessary approvals, the Committee desires 
that the Ministry should regularly monitor the progress of the above projects at 
higher levels, particularly so, as it relates to the creation of tourist infrastructure.

Crore under the PRASHAD, a total of Rs. 505.15 Crore has been released.  The 
Committee desires to be apprised of the variations, if any, between the 
sanctioned provision and the actual expenditure incurred under the PRASHAD.

training programme at various Iconic Sites i.e. Tajmahal at Agra, Humayun Tomb, 
Red Fort, Qutab Minar at Delhi, Mahabodhi Temple at Bihar, Kolva Beach at Goa 
and Kanziranga at Assam. To begin with, the  pilot of the destination-based training 
programmes have been rolled out from 13 institutes. It is proposed to expand the 
programmes to 150 tourist destinations during the year 2020-21. 
 
ii. Entrepreneurship Programme: -The objective of this programme is to  
facilitate micro and small business start -ups under the scheme of „Capacity 
Building for Service providers‟ . To begin with, 150 -hour courses are being offered 
in the five trades of (i) Cook – Tandoor , (ii) Barman, (iii) Baker, (iv) Homestay 
(Multi-Skilled Caretaker) and (v) Halwai – Indian Sweets under this Programme. 
 
iii.Online Incredible India Tourist Facilitator (IITF) :- The Ministry of Tourism 
has also initiated Incredible India Tourist Facilitator (IITF) Certification 
Programme. The objective of the Programme is to provide online training and 
accreditation of the Tour Facilitators through a centralized PAN India e -learning 
module. The institution of tourist facilitators would be a basic component of the 
infrastructural requirement both for International and Domestic tourism. There are 
two categories of IITF Certification i.e Basic & Advanced (Heritage & Adventure). 
The programme is designed in a manner that the users can learn at their own time, 
space, path and pace. The candidate/person below the age of 40 years should have 
completed 10+2 or equivalent examination whereas the candidates/persons of 40 
years of age and a bove should have completed 10 or equivalent examination 
conducted by any recognized Board by Government of India/State Government on 

 
 
47 
 
or before the date of registration to the course. Presently 2033 number of 
candidates have registered for the IITF certification Programme. 
 
117. Elaborating the reasons for doubling of budgetary allocations for the Scheme of 
Capacity Building for Service Providers in BE 2020 -21 as compared to that of RE 2019 -
20, the Ministry has inter-alia submitted that it has initiated the Destination Based Skill 
Development training programme at various Iconic Sites and the total target for the year

150 iconic sites through our imple menting agencies. It is envisaged to rollout the 
Incredible India Tourist Facilitator (IITF) programme in 2020 -21 and provide sufficient 
funds for the same.  The budgetary allocation of Rs.33.00 crores  during the financial 
year 2019 -20 was utilized to tra in 24800 persons under the skill development and 
Swachhta Action Plan (SAP) activities at 150 sites.  
 
118. India faces huge deficit in quality human resources. The Scheme – 
Assistance to IHMs/FCIs/IITTM/NIWS has been formulated to expand and 
upgrade exist ing Institutes of Hotel Management/Food Craft Institutes, Indian 
Institutes of Tourism & Travel Management, National Council for Hospitality 
and Travel Management and also to set up such new institutes to meet the 
requirements of trained manpower in the tourism and hospitality industry.  As of 
now,  46 Institutes of Hotel  Management and 14 Food Crafts Institutes have 
been set up with the support of the Ministry and one Central IHM at Jagdishpur, 
Uttar Pradesh is under construction. Against the budgetary pr ovision of Rs. 
61.00 Crore in RE 2019 -20, an amount of Rs. 49.02 Crore has been incurred as 
on 07/02/2020 under this Scheme.  The Committee apprehends that the budgeted 
funds would witness under-utilization which may have a bearing on creating and 
upgrading the institutional infrastructure for training and certification of 
manpower resources in the hospitality sector. The Committee , therefore, 
recommends that concerted efforts be made to spend the allotted money. 
119. The Committee observes that there is si gnificant potential for the tourist 
sector in India to generate jobs and absorb a substantially higher workforce.  

 
 
48 
 
However, India faces intense shortage of trained manpower at various levels of 
the tourist  sector.  It is in this context that creating appr opriate employable 
skills in the population assumes added significance.  The Committee is , therefore, 
constrained to note that there is huge variation between the annual target fixed 
and the actual achievement made in the matter of training and certification as 
the Ministry has been able to train/certify a total of 38,859 persons only under 
the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service Providers against its annual target 
of 1,01,900 persons during the year 2018 -19. The Committee desires to know the 
reasons for the same. Similarly, the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service 
Providers could not achieve its ta rgets during 2019 -20 as well.  Obviously, there 
are serious shortcomings in the implementation of the training programmes 
under CBSP.  This calls for serious introspection.  The Committee desires to be 
apprised of the remedial measures taken to overcome th e shortcomings and 
achieve the intended targets. 
120. The Committee also wishes to emphasize that the skilled workforce in the 
tourism sector should not be lost sight of and the Ministry should undertake and 
implement appropriate policy measures for absorb ing the existing certified 
trainees in the tourism and other related sectors.  The Committee desires to be 
kept apprised of the number of persons trained and employed under the various 
training skill upgradation programmes of the Ministry during 2019-20. 
121. The Committee observes that the tourism industry is very dynamic 
because of rapid changes in customer preferences and travel patterns.  The 
Committee, therefore, desires to know as to what measures have been taken to 
ensure that the various training pr ogrammes designed by the Ministry mirror 
human resources needs and are strictly need-based and demand driven. 
122. The Committee notes that the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service 
Providers is being implemented by the Ministry of Tourism through Instit utes of 
Hotel Management, Food Craft Institutes, State Governments and their training/ 
academic institutions and other stakeholders in the private sector engaged in 
imparting training in the hospitality sector.  The Committee is of the vie w that 

 
 
49 
 
CBSP, as conceived, may be unwieldy in ensuring co -ordination which has led to 
under-achievement of its targets.  It would, therefore, be necessary to have a 
formalized central coordination structure for ensuring a well -focused approach 
to the skill development initiatives under CBSP.  
123. The Committee notes that in order to scale up, the Ministry has initiated 
the Destination Based Skill Development Training Programme at various iconic 
sites and rolled it out from 13 I nstitutes. The Ministry further proposes to 
expand the programmes to 150 tourist destinations during 2020 -21.  The 
Committee desires to be apprised of the progress made in this regard. 
124. The Committee welcomes the Entrepreneurship Programme initiated as it 
is a key intervention to enable the under priviliged to set up small enterprise and 
overcome the barriers to economic participation.  The Committee expects to be 
apprised of the physical progress made under the above Programme during 
2019-20. 
125. The Committee gathers from the information made av ailable to it that the 
Ministry is considering to set up 4 Food Craft Institutes.  The Committee expects 
that all issues relating to setting up of the 4 FCIs be addressed in right earnest 
and that the funds earmarked for them be utilized fully. The Committ ee would

institutes may also be set up in rural areas to conduct training for the local 
community so that the opportunities for the poor can be expanded.   
126. The Committee is aware that there is shortage of trainers specific to 
hospitality and tourism education and that the requirement of teachers would 
continue to be large and growing.  The Committe e, therefore, desires to know as to 
how many dedicated teacher training I nstitutes have been set up under the Scheme 
Assistance to IHMs/FCIs/IITTM/NIWS and whether they are mandated to conduct 
customized training courses to cover the requirement of niche t ourism products and

VIII Cruise Tourism 
 
127. The Ministry of Tourism provides Central Financial Assistance (CFA) to the 
State Governments/UT Administrations/Central Government Agencies for 
development of Tourism including Cruise Tourism and Cruising along rivers. The 
Ministry has also sanctioned various projects for the development of Cruise Terminals 
and related infrastructure in Goa, Maharashtra, Kerala and Tamil Nadu at the major 
ports for Rs.135.72 Crore under the Scheme - „Assistance to Central Agencies for 
Tourism Infrastructure Development‟.  
 
128. The Committee has been informed that to harness the potential of cruise tourism in 
the country, a Task Force had been constituted with the Secretary (Tourism) as the 
Chairman and Secretary (Shipping) as the co -Chairman.  On the recommendations of 
Task Force, the following measures were taken for the development of cruise tourism:- 
 
 Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) have been formulated to be followed by the 
various agencies for handling cruise ships. 
 The facility of e-tourist visa has been extended to passengers arriving at the ports 
of Mumbai, Mormugao, Mangalore, Kochi and Chennai. 
 The Ministry of Home Affairs has waived off biometric requirements for cruise 
passengers arriving on e-via for a period of three year, i.e. upto 31.12.2020. 
 To address manpower, co-ordination and logistical issues for handling cruise 
vessels at ports, “Port Level Facilitation Committees” have been formed under the 
respective Chairman of the Major  Ports to facilitate seamless handling of cruise 
ships and passengers. 
 Foreign flag vessels carrying passengers have been allowed to call at Indian ports 
without obtaining licence from Director General of Shipping. 
On being asked as to why the Ministry has not utilized any other waterways, except 
for National Waterway 1 and Natio nal Waterway 2, for developing cruise circuits 
in the country and what are the difficulties faced by the Ministry in developing 
cruise tourism projects in And aman and Nicobar Islands, the Ministry has stated 
the following: 
The mandate of Inland Waterways A uthority of India (IWAI) is to develop 
and regulate National Waterways for cargo shipping & navigation.  
 
The infrastructure developed for transportation on National Waterways by 
IWAI including fairway, terminals, jetties, navigation aids etc. are used by 
the river cruise tourism operators. IWAI plays the role of a technical 
facilitator for river cruise tourism on National Waterways. 
 

 
 
51 
 
River cruise tourism has been a regular feature on National Waterway 
(NW)-1(Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system) and NW -2 (river 
Brahmaputra) since several years. Various cruise operators viz., M/s 
Heritage River Cruises Pvt. Ltd., M/s Vivada Inland Waterways and M/s 
Assam Bengal Navigation Company operate their cruise vessels on NW -1, 
NW-2 and Sunderbans waterways. 
 
National Waterway (NW) -1 (Ganga - Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system 
from Allahabad to Haldia), NW – 2 (River Brahmaputra from Dhubri to 
Sadiya), NW -3 (West Coast Canal from Kottapuram to Kollam along with 
Udyogmandal and Champakara Canals) have already been develo ped with 
fairway navigational aids, jetties and terminals with mechanized equipment 
handling facilities for loading and unloading of cargo. 
 
In addition to NW -1 & NW -2; NW -3 Kerala is a world renowned tourist 
destination for domestic and foreign tourists w here house boat tourism with 
food and accommodation facilities are available. The area of operation of 
these boats include Vembnad lake of Alapuzha, Kuttanad area and 
Astamudi lake of Kollam area. 
 
129. The Committee notes from the information made availab le to it that in the meeting 
chaired by the Prime Minister on 21 st June, 2014, it was decided that the Ministry of 
Shipping and the Ministry of Tourism would jointly identify the routes for carrying out 
cruise tours on waterways and also take measures to develop necessary infrastructure.  
Accordingly, a Working Group was  constituted to examine the modalities of cruise tours 
connecting religious places and other relate d issues.  The W orking Group has identified , 
inter alia , the following key issues and challenges pertaining to development of these 
circuits:- 
(i) Development of Infrastructure including all weather navigable channels. 
(ii) Provision of tourist amenities at terminals, jetlines, river fronts, etc., and 
(iii) Proper maintenance of tourist places. 
 
130. The Committee has also been informed that the Task Force constituted with 
Secretary (Tourism) as the Chairman and Secretary (Shipping) as the Co -Chairman 
consists of representatives from the ports, Ministry of Health, Home Affairs, External 
Affairs, Custom s, CISF, Coastal States etc. The Task Force meets regularly and has 
formulated Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) to be followed by the various agencies 
for handling of cruise ships. The Task Force has reviewed the SOPs and updated them 
into the SOP versi on 2 which is to be used for the cruise season 2017 -18. On the 

 
 
52 
 
recommendation of the Task Force, Ministry of Shipping and Ministry of Tourism have 
jointly appointed a consultant for preparing Action Plan and detailed road map for the 
development of Cruise Tourism in India. The consultants have submitted their report 
which contains many recommendations for making India a preferred destination both for 
Sea and River Cruise. The Task Force has accepted the report and decided to engage a 
Project Management Cons ultant to monitor its implementation. No projects have been 
sanctioned for development of cruise facilities to States during the year 2017 -18, 2018-19, 
2019-20.  
131. The Committee gathers that during the year 2017 -18 a total of 1,62,660 cruise 
passengers visited India at six major ports, namely, Mumbai Port, Chennai Port, Kochin 
Port, Kolkata Port, New Mangalore Port and Mormugao Port. During the same period a 
total of 139 cruise ships visited India at the six major ports. As per media reports,  the 
total cruise callings were 285 during 2018-19. 
 
132. The Committee observes that Cruise Shipping is one of the fastest growing 
components of the leisure industry world -wide.  The Indian economy is 
developing at a steady pace and became the fifth largest economy in 2019 
surpassing the U.K. and France (as per IMF‘s October 2019 World Economic 
Outlook).  India‘s middle class possessing disposal incomes is also growing in 
number. Despite all these advantages, cruise tourism in India is still in its nascent 
stage and India does not even figure in the top ten in Asia in terms of Cruise line 
port calls.  India has a mere 285 cruise calls in FY 2018 -19 whereas Thailand and 
Malaysia get about 500 cruise calls a year.  The fact remains that India‘s 
enormous cruise potential remains untapped despite being endowed with 7,500 
km of coastline.  To meet India‘s untapped cruise potential, a high level Task 
Force was constituted in the year 2015 with Secretary (Tourism) as Chairma n 
and Secretary (Shipping) as co -Chairman.  Five years have elapsed since then.  
The Task Force has reviewed and updated t he Standard Operating Procedure  
and a consultant has been jointly appointed by Ministry of Tourism and Ministry 
of Shipping for prepar ing an Action Plan and detailed blue print for the 
development of cruise tourism in the country.  It is really intriguing that despite 
acceptance of the report of the Consultant, no projects have been sanctioned for 

 
 
53 
 
development of cruise tourism to the States during 2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20. 
This, in the opinion of the Committee, speaks volumes of the Government‘s 
inertia and lethargy in the matter.   
133. Cruise Tourism is a supply -driven market and cruise lines are always in 
search of new markets and destinations.  India‘s enchanting and exotic 
destinations could catapult India as one of the leading cruise destinations.  But 
for that to happen, stable and consistent operating conditions will have to be 
concretized because cruise line companies which ty pically plan two to three years 
ahead, need to know that the basic conditions of operating are stable and 
consistent.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism 
in collaboration with Ministry of Shipping should expedite appropriate policy 
measures for developing India‘s largely untapped and hitherto small cruise 
market and pull cruise vessels to its shores.  The Committee desires to be 
updated on the progress made in this regard. 
134. The Committee also observes that many of India‘s destinations are in its 
interiors and water -based tourism is well -developed in some States like Kerala, 
Goa, West Bengal etc. However, a lot remains to be done to develop river cruise 
that connects interior tourist destinations. The Committee, therefore, d esires to 
be kept apprised of the steps taken and the achievement made towards 
developing river cruise in the country.

59 
 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism , in coordination with the

these 36 tourist routes/sectors.  The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
progress made in this regard.

accorded to transfer land and working permission has been accorded to Airport s

within the designated timeline and the approved cost, which will enable the 
tourists to reach Leh without any hassle, thereb y, contributing to improving the 
living conditions of people of Leh. 
148. The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that a total amount of 
Rs. 225 Crore has been earmarked for a period of three years for ―Extending

Scheme.  But a perusal of Demand No. 98 for 2020 -21 pertaining to the Ministry 
of Tourism reveals that an amount of Rs. 123.00 Crore has been allocated in BE 
2020-21 for the Scheme of Champion Services Sector S cheme.  Obviously, there 
is lack of clarity in this regard.  The Committee would, therefore, like the 
Ministry to explain in unambiguous terms, the dichotomy in the matter. 
149. The Committee notes that Rail is the most preferred mode of transport for 
domestic tourists.  As per the Budget (2011 -12), 26 railway stations had been 
identified for joint development of tourist amenities by the Ministry of Tourism 
and the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee notes with concern that out of the 
26 railway stations, only one has been completed and the remaining projects are

60 
 
with the Ministry of Railways , the pending issues pertaining to implementation 
of the scheme of upgradation of the 26 railway stations. Co nsidering the fact that

153. The Committee has been informed that Ministry of Tourism is seized with the issue 
to ensure safety and security of the tourists visiting the Country in general and women in

(2) Erection of signage warning visitors of the danger involved in taking selfies at 
such locations.  
(3) Posting of volunteers/tourist police at such identified places, if feasible.  
(4) Sensitization through Public Address system.  
(5) Spreading awareness through social and other media campaigns.  
(6) Barricading areas, wherever possible danger is identified.

XI India Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC) 
 
158. India Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC) is a Public Sector Undertaking 
under administrative control of the Ministry of Tourism. Incorporated on October 1, 1966, 
ITDC played a key role in the development of tourism infrastructure in the country. The 
Corporation is running hotels, restaurants at various places for t ourists, besides providing 
transport facilities. In addition, the Corporation is engaged in production, distribution and 
sale of tourist publicity literature and providing entertainment and duty -free shopping 
facilities to the tourists. The Corporation als o has its presence in engineering related 
consultancy services. ITDC was set up with a view to undertake development and 
promotion of tourism related activities. ITDC has been mandated to promote tourism in 
the country in form of infrastructure development , hotels & accommodation, travel & 
tourism promotion, printing & publicity, event management, hospitality education, Sound 
and Light Shows and other related activities. It went ahead with a view to promote 
tourism by providing quality infrastructure in pla ces where the tourism potential was 
untapped due to non-availability of accommodation, travel arrangements, etc. 
 
159. The Corporation also takes up work of execution of Engineering Projects and 
preparation of DPRs for tourism related projects. ITDC has pl ayed a committed and 
pivotal role in the development of tourism infrastructure in backward areas, thereby trying 
to promote regional balance. After the disinvestment of 09 hotels and one incomplete 
hotel project, ITDC consolidated its remaining activities and restructured itself to take up 
diversified service -oriented business activities. As per Disinvestment Policy of the 
Government of India, 9 hotel properties including 3 Joint Venture Hotel properties (viz 
Hotel Lake View Ashok, Bhopal; Hotel Brahmaputra  Ashok, Guwahati, Hotel Bharatpur 
Ashok, Bharatpur, incomplete hotel project at Gulmarg, Hotel Janpath, New Delhi, Hotel 
Jaipur Ashok, Jaipur, Lalitha Mahal Palace Hotel, Mysore, Hotel Pataliputra Ashok, Patna 
and Hotel Donyi Polo Ashok, Itanagar) have bee n transferred/ handed over to the 
respective State Governments. Disinvestment/Divestment process of remaining properties 
i.e. Process for joint leasing in respect of Hotel Pondicherry Ashok, Puducherry; Hotel 
Nilachal Ashok, Puri, process for giving Hotel Kalinga Ashok, Bhubaneswar on 
Operation & Maintenance Contract is underway. Hotel operations at Hotel Ranchi Ashok, 
Ranchi and Hotel Nilachal Ashok Puri are closed. Incomplete Project at Anandur Sahib, 
Puri is under way to be transferred to State Government. 
 
160. With the changing economic and business scenario, the Corporation is in the 
process of strengthening all business verticals to increase its turnover and profitability and 
to position itself as one stop solution for travel, tourism and hospitality needs.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS — AT A GLANCE 
 
ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2020-21 
 The Committee notes that due to broad budgetary cuts imposed by the 
Ministry of Finance, the Ministry has witnessed a reduction in allocation of funds 
for the financial year 2020 -21 and has been allocated only Rs. 2499.83 crore as 
against its projected demand of Rs. 2647.25 crore.                           (Para:23) 
 The Committee also notes that less allocation as compared to the projected 
demand is not unique to the financial year 2020-21.  Against the projected 
demands of Rs. 4320.42 Crore and Rs. 4612.18 Crore for Financial Year 2018-19 
and 2019-20 respectively, Ministry of Finance provided Rs. 2150.00 crore and Rs. 
2189.22 crore in BE 2018-19 and BE 2019-20 respectrively which were further 
reduced to Rs. 2113.48 crore and Rs. 1416.00 crore at RE 2018-19 and RE 2019-
20 stage respectively.                                                                                                  
(Para:24) 
 The Committee observes that tourism being a labour -intensive multi -
sectoral activity characterised by multiple services and industries is a key driver 
of socio -economic progress as well as employment generation and economic 
development.  The tourism sector  has the potential to stimulate other economic 
sectors through its backward and forward linkages and cross -sectoral synergies 
with sectors like agriculture, handicrafts, transport, construction, to name a few.  
It is thus evident that any higher investment  made in the tourism sector can lead 
to large sale employment generation, alleviate poverty and propel India to a 
faster growth trajectory.                            (Para:25) 
The Committee is dismayed to note that despite its unique endowments of 
biodiversity and its rich culture and heritage, India‘s total share in global 
international tourist arrivals remains a modest 1.24% against the target of 3% 
while, as per the Report of the Working Group of Tourism of the 12 th Five Year 
Plan, in about 150 countrie s of the world, tourism is one of the 5 top export 
earners and number one export earner in about 60 countries. When measured by 
the yardstick of its vast tourism resources, India‘s low share of tourism arrivals 

 
 
74 
 
is certainly below its potential.  Similarly,  the contribution (direct and indirect) 
of tourism in the GDP and the total jobs in the country is estimated to be 5.06% 
and 12.75% respectively, which, in the considered opinion of the Committee, is 
inadequate and way below the massive potential that exis ts. The Committee 
wishes to point out that in many smaller and developing countries , the entire 
economy of the country depends on tourism for its survival and tourism remains 
a major source of foreign exchange earnings. That being the case , the world's 
second largest country in terms of population, seventh largest by area, having 
7500 km of coastline and one of the most endowed regions of the world in terms 
of its tourism attractiveness, India receives less international tourists than its full 
potential.  T aking all these factors into account, the Committee apprehends that 
the shortfall of Rs. 147.42 crore in BE 2020 -21 against the projected demand of 
Rs. 2647.25 crore would seriously jeopardize the targeted tourism outcomes 
during the Financial Year 2020-21.                                                         (Para:26) 
        The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that the difference in 
the projection made by it and the allocation given for the financial year 2020 -21 
is not high and that if additional funds are required, it would move the Ministry 
of Finance for additional allocation at the RE 2020 -21 stage.  The Committee 
observes that availability of adequate resources to the tourism sector is sine qua 
non for achieving the tourism growt h as well as inclusive growth.  Since 
development of tourism infrastructure is capital intensive, the Committee 
apprehends that with the budgetary allocation of Rs.2499.83 crore for 2020 -21, 
which, in the opinion of the Committee, is low, it would be diffi cult for the 
Ministry to take up significant activities related to on -going infrastructure 
development of the sanctioned tourism circuits/destinations and also 
development of new tourism products of global standards.  If the tourism sector 
has to play a ma jor role in faster and inclusive growth, the infrastructure 
bottlenecks need to be unleashed.  The Committee notes that more than half of 
the allocation of the Ministry for 2020 -21 is devoted for the schemes relating to 
infrastructure development.  In most  of the States/UTs, the outlay for tourism is 
meagre and the Central Government has a dominance in the domain of public 

 
 
75 
 
resource mobilization by way of collection of tax revenue. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry be provided a higher financial out lay at the RE 
2020-21 stage.  The Committee would like the Ministry of Tourism to bring the 
above recommendation to the notice of Ministry of Finance and also intimate the 
Committee of their response in this regard.         (Para:27)  
    Since the consump tion demand arising from tourist expenditure has a 
multiplier effect on the economy, the expansion of the tourist sector can lead to 
large scale employment generation and  poverty alleviation. Needless to mention, 
tourism has huge potential to stimulate ove rall economic growth and any 
increase in the outlay for tourism sector can propel our country to a faster 
growth trajectory and will lead to large scale employment generation and 
alleviation of poverty. If our country can tap its full potential of the tour ism 
sector, it can play a major role for faster and inclusive growth, but for this to 
happen, the budgetary provisions for the Ministry has to be enhanced 
substantially.  By doing so, tourism infrastructure could be strengthened/

 The Committee notes with dismay the huge mismatch between the

undertaken by them are of continuous nature and that the targets are fixed and 
funds are released as per budgetary allocation by the Ministry of F inance

undertaken by them.  Tourism is important for both economic growth and

projects/schemes are not deprived of the same.       (Para:31)  
The Committee takes note of the fact that the annual growth rate of the 
Tourism Sector in India is 5.2% and its contribution to GDP is 5.06%. According 
to UN World Tourism Organisation Report (2011), for diversified economies, the 
contribution of tourism t o national GDP, is over 10% for countries where 
tourism happens to be the main driver of national economy. Quite apparently, 
despite having a strong domestic tourist base which is likely to grow further on 
the back of a rapidly rising middle class with inc reased disposable incomes and 
having many World Heritage sites and rich fauna, our country has not been able 
to exploit its tourism potential to the fullest possible extent and the tourist sector 
has not proved to be the proverbial engine of growth for our  economy. For a 

 
 
77 
 
country of our size, with wealth of attractions and experiences, this 
underperformance represents significant foregone economic value. Since tourism 
in the country has the potential to emerge as a key economic driver through 
economic growth and employment generation, the country can make a giant leap 
towards achieving 5 trillion dollar economy by tapping the enormous potential of 
the tourism sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the strategies 
adopted for promotion and developmen t of the tourist sector should be 
recalibrated to harness the full potential of Indian tourism and double the 
current contribution of tourism to GDP in the next 5 years. The Committee

trillion dollar economy by 2025 by way of a substantial contribution from the

initiated by the Ministry to accelerate the growth momentum of the tourism

CRUISE TOURISM 
 
 The Committee observes that Cruise Shipping is one of the fastest growing 
components of the leisure industry world -wide.  The Indian economy is 
developing at a steady pace and became the fifth largest economy in 2019 
surpassing the U.K. and France (as per IMF‘s October 2019 World Economic 
Outlook).  India‘s middle class possessing disposal incomes is also growing in 
number. Despite all these advantages, cruise tourism in India is still in its na scent 
stage and India does not even figure in the top ten in Asia in terms of Cruise line 
port calls.  India has a mere 285 cruise calls in FY 2018 -19 whereas Thailand and 
Malaysia get about 50 0 cruise calls a year.  T he fact remains that India‘s 
enormous cruise potential remains untapped despite being endowed with 7,500 
km of coastline.  To meet India‘s untapped cruise potential, a high level Task 
Force was constituted in the year 2015 with Secretary (Tourism) as Chairman 
and Secretary (Shipping) as co -Chairman.  Five years have elapsed since then.  
The Task Force has reviewed and updated the Standard Operating Procedure 
and a consultant has been jointly appointed by Ministry of Tourism and Ministry 
of Shipping for preparing an Action Plan and detailed blue  print for the 
development of cruise tourism in the country.  It is really intriguing that despite 
acceptance of the report of the Consultant, no projects have been sanctioned for 
development of cruise tourism to the States during 2017 -18, 2018-19 and 2019-20. 
This, in the opinion of the Committee, speaks volumes of the Government‘s 
inertia and lethargy in the matter.                             (Para:132) 
 Cruise Tourism is a supply -driven market and cruise lines are always in 
search of new markets and des tinations.  India‘s enchanting and exotic 
destinations could catapult India as one of the leading cruise destinations.  But 
for that to happen, stable and consistent operating conditions will have to be 
concretized because cruise line companies which typic ally plan two to three years 
ahead, need to know that the basic conditions of operating are stable and 
consistent.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism 
in collaboration with Ministry of Shipping should expedite appropriate pol icy 
measures for developing India‘s largely untapped and hitherto small cruise 

 
 
88 
 
market and pull cruise vessels to its shores.  The Committee desires to be 
updated on the progress made in this regard.               (Para:133)

be kept apprised of the steps taken and the achievement made towards 
developing river cruise in the country.                (Para:134)

 The Committee takes note  of the other measures initiated by the Ministry 
of Tourism such as a 24 7 Multi-Lingual Tourist Info -Helpline, adoption of the 
Code of Conduct for ‗Safe and Honourable Tourism,‖ and Guidelines on Safety 
and Security of Tourists to ensure that widespread a wareness on issues related to 
good behaviour towards tourists, civic responsibilities and security and comfort 
of tourists is generated.  The Committee desires to be apprised of the efficacy of 
these measures in bringing about an attitudinal change towards tourists.                 
           (Para:157) 
INDIA TOURISM DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION (ITDC) 
 The Committee notes that ITDC has registered a total turnover of Rs. 
371.72 crore in the financial year 2018 -19. It reported a profit before tax (PBT) 
of Rs. 57.91 crore during this period as compared to Rs. 21.25 crore in the 
corresponding period last year, clocking an increase of 63.30 %. It registered 
profit after tax (PAT) of Rs. 42.15 crore compared to 17.71 crore in the previous 
financial year. Since one simple way to determine if a company has a good return 
on equity is to compare it to the average of its industry, the Committee desires to 
be apprised of ITDC's Return on Equity (ROE) and how the same compares with 
the average ROE in the hospitality sector.     (Para:171)  
 The Committee notes that as per the Disinvestment Policy of the 
Government of India, 9 hotel properties including 3 joint venture properties have 
been transferred/handed over to the respective State Governments. The 
Committee observes th at in modern times , the success of hospitality business 
hinges on distribution and digital strategy. Distribution means having a wide 
portfolio of hotels - budget, mid -market, upscale, luxury, etc. - at key 
destinations. By transferring the management of these 9 hotels to St ate 
Governments who will run them as individual units, these hotels will lack the 


 
 
92 
 
distribution strength that all the branded hotel chains - foreign or domestic - 
have been building. The Committee recommends that ITDC should reorient its 
strategy towards ma ximising the revenue by leveraging resources of its existing 
hotels through Public Private Partnership and consolidation of existing 
businesses.               (Para:172) 
 The Committee notes that for the financial year 2019 -20 the revised 
budget estimates for capital outlay was Rs. 17.75 crore which includes renovation 
of Hotel properties and catering units for Rs. 15.80 crore. The Committee 
observes that renovation and upgradation of hotel prope rties is a continuous 
activity. However, as a consequence of D isinvestment, no real attention has been 
given for upgradation and renovation of ITDC's hotel properties. The Committee 
is, therefore, of the considered opinion that in order to remain competitive and 
match the standards of the private players, ITDC would require more funding 
support from the Government of India. Since share capital of ITDC is small and 
not adequate to carry out major capital expenditures and capital ventures, the 
Committee recommends that the Government of India should provide more 
funding support to ITDC by way of equity infusion. The Committee desires to be 
kept apprised of the action taken in its regard.                  (Para:173)     
 The Committee also recommends that ITDC should undertake detailed 
manpower study in all its units/ divisions so that deployment of human resources 
could be rationalized.                            (Para:174)  
MISCELLANEOUS 
 The Committee notes that the Working Group on Tourism of the 12 th Five 
Year Plan , in its Report , had suggested a number of strategies regarding 
development of the tourism sector like infrastructure, connectivity, human 
resource development and capacity augmentation, convergence among various 
agencies at Centre and State level for development of touri sm, taxation, 
incentives and facilitation of tourism sector etc.  The Committee desires to be 
apprised of the extent to which those recommendations have been taken into 

 
 
93 
 
consideration by the Ministry while formulating its Policies and Programmes. 
                                                                                 (Para:175) 
 The Committee feels that each State Government has a responsibility to 
identify and reserve suitable Government land for development of potential 
tourist locations and the l and so reserved should not be used for any other 
purposes other than for constructing hotels, shopping complexes, etc.  The 
Central Government should also play a pivotal role in this regard. Central 
Ministries may also be advised to explore the possibility  of identifying and 
reserving idle land for development of tourist locations.                          (Para:176)  
 In order to promote tourism, the Committee would like the Ministry to act 
as a catalyst for building more amusement/theme parks on the lines  of the Essel 
World, Mumbai and Disneyland, California.  In the coming years, such parks 
may be built in big metropolitan cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and funds 
should be earmarked for the purpose.               (Para:177)
  The progress of implementa tion of projects sanctioned by the 
Ministry should be monitored on a monthly basis by a High Powered Project 
Monitoring Committee  and it should be ensured that the funds released for the 
sanctioned projects do not remain idly parked , but are utilised prod uctively for 
the intended purpose  and a monthly Progress Report  be submitted to the 
Minister for suitable direction, whenever the Projects are lagging behind.  
(Para:178)  
 The Committee notes from the information furnished , that our country 
has targeted to increase its share in global tourist arrivals from the current 
1.24% to 3% and double the number of domestic tourist visits from the current 
1854.9 million to 3200 million visits.  If these ambitious targets are to be met,  the 
country has to create appropriate employable skill in the population and also 
reduce the skill -gap.  The State Governments are major stakeholders in human 
resource and skill development.  The Committee would, therefore, recommend 
that the Ministry in co-ordination with the State Governments , should formulate 
a multipronged approach to bridge the skill gap in the tourism sector and should 

 
 
94 
 
also launch a programme to upgrade the skills of the existing tourist service 
providers.                                                                 (Para:179)  
 The Committee notes that the Scheme of Swadesh Darshan was launched 
with the objective of developing tourist circuits on specific themes and as of now, 
15 such Circuits have been identified for Integrated I nfrastructure Development. 
Since the creation of tourist infrastructure leads to overall economic growth, the 
Committee would like the Ministry to identify more tourism circuits and develop 
them in an integrated manner.                           (Para:180)  
 The Committee notes that there is lack of reasonably priced 
accommodation near the tourist destinations in the country. Expensive 
accommodation is a big deterrent not only for international tourists , but also for 
domestic tourists. The Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to take up 
with the State Governments , the issue of promotion of Home Stays and earmark 
funds for the same so that the widening gap between supply and demand of the 
accommodation sector could be easily bridged.             (Para:181)
                     
 The Committee notes that most of the international and domestic tourists 
visit enchantingly beautiful Kerala which is famous for its beautiful backwaters, 
unique culture and traditions and rich vegetation. The State is one o f the most 
popular tourist destinations of the world. From the information made available, 
it seems that no major tourism project has been sanctioned for the State of 
Kerala in the recent past.  The Committee, therefore, desires to know whether 
any tourist  project forwarded by the State Government of Kerala for funding 
support from the Ministry of Tourism is pending approval. The Committee also 
recommends that the approval to any such pending projects should be expedited. 
                          (Para:182) 
 The Committee observes that cruise tourism in India is a niche product to 
promote and attract tourists with specific interest. The Committee would, 
therefore, like the Ministry of Tourism to work in coordination with Ministry of 

 
 
95 
 
Shipping towards establi shing dedicated cruise terminals at all the major ports 
and also private ports in the country.                (Para:183)  
 The Roads and Highway networks play an important role in tourism and 
also in the growth of Indian economy. The Committee is aware that the Ministry 
of Road Transport and Highways had taken up detailed review of National 
Highways network with a view to improve the road connectivity to tourist places. 
The Committee desires to be apprised of the progress made so far in this regard.  
                     (Para:184)  
 The Committee recommends that under the PRASHAD, the Ministry 
should develop a dedicated thoroughfare for use by pedestrians visiting 
Srisailam. The Araku Valley and Lambasing in Visakhapatnam has great 
tourism significance and should be developed as tourist spots.  (Para:185)  
 The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministries of Civil Aviation, 
Shipping, Road Transport & Highways, Culture, Tourism and  Railways  are not 
only inter -related and interconnected but also have a common objective to 
improve connectivity and better amenities for the benefit of tourists, travellers 
and faster movement of freight within the country. The Committee, therefore, 
feels that there is a pressing need for having an effective co -ordination 
mechanism among these Ministries so that the policies and guidelines being 
formulated by them are executed seamlessly and can supplement each other in 
achieving these objectives. This will not only increase effectiveness and efficiency, 
but will also help in utilization of funds and skilled manpower to the maximum 
possible extent. Therefore, the Committee recommends that an easy -to-use 
interface should be made available which allows hassl e-free communication and 
co-ordination amongst them. A hotline number which is common to all these 
Ministries, may be established so that whenever emergency arises, there can be 
effective and prompt coordination among these Ministries and issues in hand ca n 
be resolved at the earliest.                                                                   (Para:186) 
 Belum Caves in Kurnool District which are the second largest caves on the 
Indian subcontinent, have immense tourism value and are, therefore, of na tional 

 
 
96 
 
importance.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the above Caves should 
be developed under the  Swadesh Darshan Scheme (SDS).    (Para:187)  
 Since religious tourism is an important segment of domestic tourism, the 
Committee recommends that Kolanu Bharati Saraswati Temple, Mahanandi, 
Ahobilam, Yaganti Uma Maheshwar Temple, Veera Brahman Gaari Matham, 
should be developed under Spiritual Circuit o f Swadesh Darshan Scheme.  The 
Committee also recommends that Mantralayam Raghavendra Swamy Varri 
Temple, Tumblam Jain and Ram Temple and Urukunda Eeranna Temple (Sri 
Narasimha Eranna Swamy Temple) in Kurnool District should be developed 
under PRASHAD Scheme.                   (Para:188) 
 The Committee has come to know that th e State Government of Telangana 
has sent a proposal for development of Alampur - Jagulambha Temple, which is 
one of the Shakti Peethams, located in Telangana. For this, the Committee 
recommends that Telangana's proposal should be considered promptly and that 
the above scheme should be included for its development under PRASHAD 
Scheme.                                                                                                  (Para:189) 
 The Committee notes that an allocation of Rs. 450 Crore has been made in 
BE 2020 -21 under the Scheme of Overseas Promotion and - Publicity for 
promotion of Indian tourism in overseas source markets.  The Committee 
recommends that an audit may be carried out to assess the efficacy of expenditure 
in promoting tourism in overseas source market and it should be ensured that 
value from money is derived from the money spent under the above head. 
                           (Para:190) 
 The Committee recom mends that an audit of the expenditure incurred 
under the various tourism schemes should be conducted to make the 
implementation of these programmes effective so that actual benefits reach the 
intended target groups and delivery systems are improved. Invol vement of Local 
Member of Parliament could add value to the features of various programmes of 
the Ministry.                       (Para:191) 

 
 
97 
 
 The Committee has been informed that the State Government of Arunachal 
Pradesh has forwarded proposals for develop ment of Vismak Nagar, Dibang 
Valley District and Malani Tan, Lower Siang District in Arunachal Pradesh for 
inclusion under the PRASHAD Scheme.  The Committee lends its support for the 
same and recommends their inclusion and development under the PRASHAD 
Scheme.                                                    (Para:192) 
 The Committee also recommends inclusion of Srirangapatna, Melukote, 
Mandya District (Karnataka) for inclusion and development under the 
PRASHAD Scheme.                             (Para:193) 
 The Committee takes note of the submission of the Ministry that no project 
under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme is pending for scrutiny by the Central 
Sanctioning & Monitoring Committee and observes that the above submission is 
factually incorrect.  The Committee has been informed that several proposals sent 
by the State Governments for inclusion under the SDS are pending approval by 
the Ministry of Tourism.  The Committee desires to be furnished with a list of 
such proposals indicating the date of their receipt in the Ministry, action taken 
thereon and shortcomings, if any, noticed.  The Committee also desires to know 
whether the concerned Governments have been informed about the shortcomings 
noticed in this regard.                   (Para:194)  
 The Comm ittee observes that to overcome the aspect of seasonality and 
promote India as a 365 -days tourism destination, it is necessary that the potential 
of adventure tourism is harnessed fully.  To give a fillip to the growth of 
adventure tourism, it is important  that adventure tourism activities like 
paragliding, parasailing, aero -sports including skydive etc. are encouraged.  The 
Committee is, however, constrained to note that no dedicated budgetary provision 
has been made in BE 2020 -21 of the Ministry for promo tion of the above said 
activities.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient outlay be 
earmarked for the adventure tourism activities including paragliding, parasailing, 
aero sports etc.                                                                                                 (Para:195) 

 
 
98 
 
The Prime Minister has taken keen interest to promote the tourism sector 
of our country globally.  In view of this, the Committee urges that the 
Ambassadors should take the initiative to propagate the idea of the Prime 
Minister of making India a major tourism hub.  The Ministry of External Affairs 
should also post an exclus ive tourism officer in all the E mbassies for doing the 
same.  The Ambassador should also conduct regular meeting s with the 
stakeholders on the measures taken by the Government to promote tourism and 
also direct the officials posted in the E mbassies to make the local public aware of 
the immense pot ential of the country‘s tourism. Committee desires that the 
feedback so received may be sent to  the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism via 
Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs to enable the Tourism Ministry to act on 
the feedback.                    (Para:196)
