REPORT 
The Ministry of Civil Aviation is responsible for the formulation of national policies 
and programmes for the development and regulation of the Civil Aviation sector in the 
country. It is responsible for the administration of the Aircraft Act, 1934, Aircraft Rules, 
1937 and various other legislations pertaining to the aviation sector in the country. 
2. In addition to primary functions of framing of policies, the Ministry provides 
guidance to the organizations in the implementation of policy guidelines, monitors and 
evaluates their activities and also provides their interface with Parliament. It also supervises 
implementation by the organizations of special programmes of the Government, particularly 
those intended for the weaker sections of society. 
 3. The Ministry of Civil Aviation  has the following organizations under its 
administrative control:- 
(i) Attached Offices /Organizations 
 Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) 
 Bureau of Civil Aviation Authority (BCAS) 
 Commission of Railway Safety (CRS) 
 Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) 
(ii) Autonomous Bodies 
 Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA) 
 Airports Economic Regulatory Authority (AERA) 
 Rajiv Gandhi National Aviation University (RGNAU) 
(iii) Public Sector Undertakings 
 Airports Authority of India (AAI) 
 Air India Limited (AIL) 
 Pawan Hans Limited (PHL) 
4. The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism 
and Culture considered Demand No.8 containing the details of budget allocations of the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation for the financial year 2020 -21 at it s meeting held on the 20 th 
February, 2020. During the meeting, the Committee heard the views of the Secretary and 
other senior officers of the Ministry as well as the Heads of the organizations under its 
purview, mainly on budgetary aspects  and incidental aspects relating thereto.

activities under Revenue Section  of the Ministry will be affected. In order to meet the 
requirement for the on -going projects of the Ministry, proposals will be taken up in th e first 
Supplementary and RE 2020 -21. In response to a query as to how the Ministry proposes to 
utilize the proposed budgetary allocation, the Secretary, while deposing before the 
Committee, stated that out of Rs. 3480.42 crores (Schemes), Rs. 810.23 crore s will be spent 
for purchase of two VVIP aircrafts, Rs. 2205 crores has been given to Air India for service of 
debts and the rest will be utilized for other activities. 
13.3. The Committee notes that compared to BE 2019 -20 of Rs. 4500 crores and Rs. 
3700 crores at RE 2019-20, Rs. 3797.71 crores has been allocated to the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation for 2020-21.  Elaborating the reasons for the reduction of Rs. 800 crores at RE 
stage, the Secretary clarified that the delivery of two Special Extra Section Fligh t 
(SESF) VVIP aircrafts which were bought through Air India have been rescheduled 
from January, 2020 to June, 2020 and  hence this reduction. The Committee notes that 
the Capital side allocation had remained the same, whereas, on the revenue side , more 
than 50% of allocation is meant for servicing the debt of Air India and Purchase of 2 
VVIP Planes and  the remaining allocation is available for other activities of the 
Ministry.  Keeping in view the security threat prevailing in the aviation sector all over 
the world, the Committee is of the considered view that the inadequacy of budgetary 
allocation would hamper vital activities, such a s installation of body scanners and  
provision of Capital for Rohini Heliport . The Committee feels that it is high time for 
installation of body scanners at all the airports in the country and therefore, fund 
allocation to the Ministry be substantially increased at the R.E. stage for the purpose.

Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) 
15. The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, while deposing before the Committee, 
stated thus: 
".....I would like to say that there is a small challenge before us which I would 
like to bring to the notice of the Committee.  This Carbon Offsetting and 
Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) has said that airlines 
pollute.  They burn fuel, so they pollute.  So, this is said that whatever we 
pollute in the year 2020 will become our benchmark, and beyond that, if we 
pollute, we will have to buy carbon credits.  Now, this has serious implications 
for our aviation industry in the sense that we are still a growing industry.  The 
European and American airlines have reached their peak, but we are still 
expanding.  So, we will be capped at a very low level.  In future, when we 
expand, we will have to buy carbon credits.  We have to take this up 
diplomatically.  We are trying to change the entire thing.  At different fora, it 
is being discussed internationally.  I t is our attempt that this has to be 
postponed, but it is a serious concern for the aviation industry in India....". 
15.1. The Committee notes that a serious challenge is awaiting the nation, in the ever 
expanding aviation industry, after 2020 i.e., with regard to buying of carbon credits.  As 
more and more areas are connected and expansion takes place, Ministry will have  to 
buy a lot of carbon credit, which will invol ve huge financial implications. Under these 
circumstances, the Committee desires the Minis try to have a study of the financial 
implications involved for future expansion of our aviation sector which is presently at a 
nascent stage, but has a huge  potential for further expansion. The Comm ittee also calls 
upon the Ministry to take up  this issue , diplomatically as well as politically , at the 
highest possible level, to sort it out as early as possible  so as to secure  the future of our 
civil aviation industry.

Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS) 
16. The Ministry has launched RCS -UDAN scheme on 21.1 0.2016 to facilitate/stimulate 
regional air connectivity and making air travel affordable to the masses. With the objective of 
promoting affordability being at the core, under RCS, airline operators would be offered 
concessions by Central Government, State  Governments and airport operators and financial 
support (Viability Gap Funding) to meet the gap, if any, between the cost of airline 
operations and expected revenues on regional routes. The interested airlines based on their 
assessment of demand on partic ular routes submit proposals at the time of bidding under 
RCS. As per the Ministry's reply, under three rounds of bidding, out of 688 valid RCS 
Routes, 256 RCS routes commenced as on 08-02-2020 connecting 48 airports/ heliports.

16.4. On the issue of Seamless integration of places of tourist and cultural importance under 
the RCS, the Ministry submitted that extensive co nsultations with line Ministries are done 
under Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS) –Ude Desh Ka Aam Nagrik, (UDAN), 
especially with Ministry of Tourism and Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region. 
In the 3 rd round of bidding under RCS -UDAN, 46 Tourism routes have been awarded to 
selected Airline Operators (SAOs) on the request of Ministry of Tourism. Out of these, 14 
routes have commenced as on 08.02.2020. Ministry of Tourism has agreed to pay 100% of 
Viability Gap Funding (VGF) for these routes . However, funds are yet to be received from 
M/o Tourism. 
16.5. The Committee notes that RCS has given the Indian aviation industry a huge 
fillip. This Scheme has made air travel more affordable and also the connectivity to 
remote and hilly regions of the country has improved.  The Committee notes that 
availability of funds and high cost of operations are the major constraints under the 
Scheme.  The Committee finds that out of 688 valid routes awarded, only 256 rout es 
have commenced operations, which constitute only 37% of the awarded routes.  Despite 
the fact that the Ministry frequently conducts bidding for RCS routes and awards 
routes, desired progress ha s not taken place.  Given the tremendous enthusiastic 

12 
 
response from the stakeholders including the pas sengers and significant change noticed 
in the economic activity of the connected routes with current level of 37% routes, there 
is a huge potential in terms of connectivity and the resultant economic prosperity  under 
the Scheme.  The Committee, therefore, desires that concerted efforts should be made to 
operationalize all the awarded routes at the earliest. The Committee also desires  that 
periodic evaluation of the Scheme be conducted to address the constraints of the issues 
in implementation.   
16.6. The C ommittee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry for seamless 
integration of places of tourist and cultural importance at 46 Tourism routes out of 
which only 14 have actually operationalised , which is only 30% of the identified routes.  
The Ministry needs to operationalize the remaining routes, as this will not only generate 
substantially huge financial resources, but also bear huge employment potential. The 
Committee desires that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should actively pursue with the 
Ministry of Tourism, for early release of  100% VGF for the above mentioned routes.

Shortage of pilots 
26. The following steps have been taken by DGCA to enhance the availability of pilots:- 
(i)  There is the shortage of type r ated commanders in the country due to growth in 
aviation industry and induction of new type of aircraft in the fleet by the airline. Though 
sufficient numbers of Indian Co -pilot are available and employed by the airlines, they do not 
possess the level of s kill and experience the commander s require on the latest fleet of 
aircrafts. To cover the shortage of type rated pilots, validation of foreign pilots is done as per 
Rule 45 of Aircraft Rules, 1937. As per their policy , the expat pilots are phased out by th e 
airlines once the Co-pilots inducted by them become eligible for commander after undergoing 
requisite training for the same . The present policy of hiring foreign pilots by Airlines has 
been extended up to 31.12.2020 by the Central Government. 
(ii)  The c ondition of having flying experience in preceding Five years for issue of 
Commercial Pilot Licence has been done away with by amending Section J of Schedule II of 
The Aircraft Rules, 1937 (containing the requirements for the issue of Commercial Pilot 
Licence) so that more number of aspiring pilots after completing the requisite number of 
flying hrs and undergoing recency and skill test, may now apply for the issue of CPL. 
(iii)   In order to have more number of experienced instructors and examiners with the  
Flying Training Organization (FTO) an amendment in Section Q & R of Schedule II of 
Aircraft Rule 1937 {containing the requirements for the issue of Assistant Flight Instructor 
(AFIR) and Flight Instructor Rating (FIR) respectively} has been carried out. B y easing out 
amendment in Section Q&R, more CPL holder can apply for AFIR & FIR and the shortage of 
Instructors / examiners in FTO will be addressed. Subsequently, after acquiring more 
experience, these Instructors / examiners can apply for FTO. 
(iv)  DGCA has also made provision for conversion of AFIR/FIR Ratings obtained on the 
foreign licence to ensure the availability of more Instructors. 
(v)  DGCA has also amended the flying experience requirements for issue of Airlines 
Transport Pilots Licence (Aeroplane/Helicopter) by amending the Section N &M of Schedule 

18 
 
II of Aircraft Rules, 1937 containing the requirements for the issue of ATPL. By amendments 
in Section M & N more Co -pilots may get ATPL and may become eligible for Pilot -in 
command and more number of defence pilot will become eligible to get ATPL.

to  shortage of type rated commanders in the country. The Committee strongly feels

is just a matter of time and effort that these resources are tapped into.

Ministry of Civil Aviation and had its functional administrative office for running the 
services entrusted to it on behalf of the Government at  the premises of Safdarjung, was 
evicted by AAI. It was also noted that the ACI building constructed at the Safdarjung 
Airport was done by the own resources of the Aero Club of India. The Committee 
observes that the legacy of ACI, which goes back to pre -independence times, even when 
it has been noted that the first commercial license issued in the country, prior to the 
formation of DGCA and the Ministry of Civil Aviation, both before independence and 
after independence has been completely eroded with its om ission from the budget 
document and the Annual Report as well. It strongly suggests that all the 
aforementioned points be addressed by the Ministry. 
(Para 27.5) 
Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA) 
 The Committee appreciates the roadmap formulated for IGRUA and hopes that 
the implementation of the roadmap will revive IGRUA which is beset with various 
problems. The Committee desires that periodic updates may be furnished to it on the 
steps taken for improvements in the domain of IGRUA. 
(Para 28.1) 
Air Sewa initiative 
 From the above table, the Committee finds that some grievances of passengers 
are pending from 2016 and that a large number of them i.e., 1065 grievances belong  to 
2019.  The Committee feels that this is not a healthy sign.  The Committee, therefore, 
urges the Ministry to resolve all the pending grievances at the earliest and that a status 
note should be furnished to the Committee. The Committee , however, appreciates the 
fact that the Ministry is planning to upgrade its Air Sewa Platform to meet passengers’ 
requirements.  The Committee hopes that the upgraded platform will go a long way in 
resolving the grievances of passengers. 
(Para 29.3) 
Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) facilities in India  
 The Committee is aware of the huge potential that India has, in offering MRO 
facilities in its soil. It is a sad fact that India could not fully exploit the opportunities 
available in this sector.  MRO, being a sunrise  industry, and with our huge technical 
and skill base, by creating a congenial environment, India can easily meet the 
requirements of the sector.  By giving boost to this sector, new employment 
opportunities can be created for our fresh engineering student s. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly feels that the Ministry should give adequate and immediate focus on 
the issues faced in the MRO sector and chalk out strategic measures to make positive 
interventions in order to ensure that India becomes a key player in offering MRO 

36 
 
facilities. This will also help in achieving the Prime Minister’s vision of attaining 5 
trillion economy. 
(Para 30.1) 
Air Cargo sector 
 The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry unveiled its National Air 
Cargo Policy in January, 2019  which includes some good initiatives like the first -in-
world dedicated Air Flight corridors between India -Afganistan which is proposed to be 
extended to all and land -locked countries in a phased manner.  The Committee would 
like the Ministry to initiate c oncrete actions in that direction , for it will encourage code 
sharing/interline agreements between foreign and Indian carriers. 
(Para 31.1) 
 The Committee is of the view that India has a huge untapped market potential in 
the sector and it is high time to b ring about policy and structural changes aimed 
towards transparency and paperless trade environment in this sector. 
(Para 31.2) 
Krishi UDAN 
 The Committee welcomes the launching of this new Scheme and hopes that its 
operationalisation will assist farmers to a large extent in timely transportation of 
agricultural products to the destined places of trade.  This Scheme, if implemented in 
right earnest, will cut down the losses of farmers to a major extent and also  help in 
reducing waste. The Committee would l ike to be kept updated in the status of the 
Scheme and its implementation. 
(Para 32.1) 
Remotely Piloted aircraft system (RPAS) commonly known as drones 
 The Committee takes note of the increasing number of drones in the country and 
calls upon the Ministry to establish an effective Drone Traffic Management System. The 
Committee would also like the regulatory mechanism to be strengthened for this 
purpose. 
(Para 33.1) 
High cost of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) 
 The Committee welcomes the step taken by St ate Governments in reducing the 
VAT on ATF for the flights operated under UDAN Scheme. The State Governments  
have shown reluctance to reduce the VAT on ATF for other flights. The Committee 
feels that this issue needs urgent attention to bring much needed relief and help in 
flourishing the Aviation Sector. The Committee is of the view that the issue of inclusion 
of ATF under GST should be pursued vigorously with the State Governments. 
(Para 34.1) 
Digi Yatra 
 The Committee welcomes Digi Yatra initiative in the domain of security. Digi 
Yatra will not only facilitate paperless travel , but also ensure hassle free mo vement of 
passengers at  multiple points at the airports. 
(Para 35.1) 
Aircraft Leasing and Financing from India 
 The Committee is of the view that t aking into account the thriving aviation 
industry in India, the regulatory framework relating to financing and leasing of 
aircrafts should be given a fresh look. This is vital to the sustainable and cost effective 
growth of the aviation industry in India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a 

37 
 
detailed study may be conducted in this regard and that a plan of action may be chalked 
out at the earliest. 
(Para 36.3) 
Faulty Engines 
 The Committee is satisfied with the action taken by the Ministry. At the same 
time, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure that the airlines may 
purchase engines which have been in the market for a stipulated, reasonable period of 
time with credentials of international safety standards. The Committee also desi res that 
AAIB should assess the reasons for such engine failure and recommend suitable 
remedial measures. The Committee desires the Ministry to frame safety standards/ 
protocols in aircraft operations. 
(Para 37.1) 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministr y should ensure that aircrafts and 
helicopters which have at least 3 year flying exposure, should be considered for 
purchase, when it is used for commercial purposes. 
(Para 37.2) 
Emergency landing and cancellation of flights 
 The Committee is anguished that the air travelers get a rough deal, instead of 
care and attention, in cases of emergency landings and cancellation of flights by airlines. 
It is the obligation of the airlines to ensure the comfort and health of the passenge rs, 
especially women, children and patients. The Ministry should urgently frame the 
Guidelines to be scrupulously adhered to by the airlines with a clear provision for 
punitive action in case of violation of the guidelines.  
(Para 38.1) 
Air Connectivity/Helicopter Services 
 The Committee recommends the Ministry to adopt a futuristic approach in 
connecting important tourist destinations in the country. The Committee emphasizes 
the need to ensure adequate infrastructure and facilities at such airports/helipor ts. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry should bolster its efforts to enhance 
airport network by providing more Water-drones. 
(Para 39.1) 
Cancellation charges 
 The Committee notes that there is no uniformity in the cancellation charges 
levied by the airlines. The Committee lends its support to the demand of rationalising 
the cancellation charges and is of the view that the airlines may be persuaded to restrict 
not more than 50% of the base fare as cancellation charges. The tax and fuel surcharge 
collected should be refunded to the passengers on cancellation of tickets.  The 
Committee hopes that the Ministry would be able to persuade the airlines for such 
rationalisation in the interest of the passengers. 
(Para 40.1) 
Insufficiency of hangars 
 The Committee is of the considered view that since the Ministry is taking 
commendable steps to ensure air connectivity to remote areas also, it is an essential 
corollary that well equipped hangars are also built in such places, in order to ensure 
proper and time efficient maintenance of aircrafts and helicopters. 
(Para 41.1) 
 

38 
 
Air India Ltd. 
 As the Government has already fast tracked the disinvestment of Air India, the 
Committee would like the Ministry to furnish a status note  within one month from the 
date of submission of this Report to the Parliament. 
(Para 42.2) 
Need for better co-ordination between Ministries 
 The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministries of Civil Aviation, Shipping, 
Road Transpor t & Highways, Culture, Tourism and Railways  are not only inter -
related and interconnected , but also have a common objective to improve connectivity 
and better amenities for the benefit of tourists, travellers and faster movement of freight 
within the country. The Committee, therefore, strongly advocates a pressing need for 
having an effective co-ordination mechanism among these Ministries so that the policies 
and guidelines being formulated by them are executed seamlessly a nd can supplement 
each other in achieving these objectives. This will not only increase effectiveness and 
efficiency, but will also help in utilization of funds and skilled manpower to the 
maximum possible extent. Therefore, the Committee recommends that a n easy -to-use 
interface should be made available which allows hassle -free communication and co -
ordination amongst them. A hotline number which is common to all these Ministries, 
may be established so that whenever emergency arises, there can be effective a nd 
prompt coordination among these Ministries and issues in hand can be resolved at the 
earliest. 
(Para 43) 
Air ambulance 
 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should give urgent and 
adequate attention to the growing need of Air Ambulance services in the country . The 
Committee desires that necessary policies and guidelines may be formulated in this 
regard. 
(Para 44.1) 
Commission of Railway Safety (CRS) 
 The Committee observes that it would be in the fitness of jurisdiction and 
administrative convenience that  the headquarters of the Commissioner of Railway 
Safety should be shifted from Lucknow to New Delhi for facilitating better logistics and 
coordination. The Commission may function as an independent entity and directly 
Report to the Minis ter of Civil Aviation through Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation. 
The Committee desires that necessary manpower and infrastructure may be provided 
at the earliest, for smooth functioning of the Commission. The Committee also desires 
that the status of C ommissioner of Railway Safety may be upgraded , as recommended 
by the Committee in its 188th Report. 
(Para 45.1) 
Multi Member Consultative Committee  
 The Committee recommends that the MMCC should work out ways to 
empower CRS and to sort out issues presently existing in the effective functioning of 
CRS.  
(Para 46.1) 
Core group on Safety and Security  
 The Committee emphasizes the need for a combined robust security framework 
to ensure safety and security in sectors of Civil Aviation, Road Transport & Highways, 

39 
 
Shipping, Tourism and Railways. The Committee desires that in order to facilitate 
effective and periodic coordination among the concerned Ministries and agencies, a core 
group comprising officers at the level of Joint Secretary of the Ministries of Civil 
Aviation, Road Transport & Highways, Shipping, Tourism, Railways , Commissioner of 
Railway Safety  and Petroleum may be set up to meet on monthly basis to chalk out 
ways and means for addressing safety and security concerns in these sectors and ensure 
that international best practices are followed. This core group should be headed by 
Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation. In order to upgrade to international standards, 
the services of consultants (both domestic and international) who are experts in the 
respective fields and have domain knowledge, may be engaged for preparing Reports so 
that they can be implemented. This core group may serve as a think-tank and formulate 
guidelines and directions to improve safety and security standards in these sectors. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to furnish the monthly Reports and status of 
implementation of its decisions, to the Committee. 
(Para 47) 
Miscellaneous  
The Committee notes that Patna needs a Greenfield project to cater to the 
growing traffic demand of the state, for domestic and international passengers and can 
emerge as the largest hub of Aviation in the Eastern Sector. It will also be beneficial to 
passenger traffic to the South -Eastern Corridor, the Middle East and act as a diversion 
airport for Kathmandu. This proposed airport shall serve as a major hub for Buddhist 
and Sikh pilgrims on the Bihar religious tourism circuit. 
(Para 48.1)

INTRODUCTION 
Culture is the focal point around which the identity of a nation and its people gets 
established. Culture comprises the customary beliefs, social forms and material traits of a 
racial, religious or social group. Culture plays a pivotal role in establishing the uniqueness 
of a country especially in these times of globalization. Shared culture acts as a unifying 
factor among the citizens. A well -preserved, unique and vibrant culture of a nation is 
directly linked with its t ourism prospects and thus , frames a key component in the 
developmental agenda of any nation. 
2.  The primary mandate of Ministry of Culture is preservation and conservation of 
ancient cultural heritage and promotion of tangible and intangible art and culture.  Headed 
by Secretary, the administrative set up consists of 5 Bureaus and Divisions. The Ministry 
has two attached offices, six subordinate offices and thirty five autonomous organisations, 
which are fully funded by the Government which include seven Zonal  Cultural Centres. 
There are also four missions viz., the National Mission for Manuscripts, National Mission 
for Monument and Antiquities, National Mission on Libraries, and Gandhi Heritage Sites 
Mission.  
3.  This Ministry work s on the protection, developmen t and promotion of the country‟s 
tangible heritage, intangible heritage and knowledge heritage. In addition, the Ministry 
also harbours the responsibility of nurturing Gandhian heritage and commemoration of 
important historical events and centenaries of gr eat personalities. The Ministry manages 
all the Centrally protected monuments of national importance, through the Archaeological 
Survey of India. It supports museum movement in the country and majority of the 
museums are under its administrative control. T he Ministry also promotes regional 
museums through grant -in-aids. In the field of intangible heritage, the Ministry extends 
financial support to individuals, group of individuals and cultural organizations involved 
with the performing, visual and literary arts. Similarly, the Ministry through its 
organizations, is engaged in recognizing excellence in the field of art and culture by way 
of awards given by institutions like Sahitya Akademi and Sangeet Natak Akademi. The 
National School of Drama is involved in  promoting a vibrant theatre movement of 
contemporary relevance in the context of our traditions and cultural diversity. 
4.  The Ministry is the custodian of all the major libraries in the country. It frames 
policies and provides grants -in-aid for library dev elopment. Through National Archives 
of India, Ministry is responsible for maintenance of all archival records of the country. 
The Ministry protects and promotes Buddhist and Tibetan Culture through institutions 
located at Sarnath, Varanasi and Leh. Capacity building programmes in the field of Indian 
art and culture is promoted through institutions like the School of Archaeology, School of 
Archives, National Museum , Institute of History of Art, Conservation and Museology, 
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Institute of  Asian Studies. The courses offered by National 
School of Drama and Kalakshetra Foundation are also some of the examples of capacity 
building programmes of the Ministry.  

2 
 
5.  On the international front, the Ministry is responsible for implementation of variou s 
UNESCO Conventions and for entering into Cultural Exchange Agreements with 
partnering countries.

13.  The Committee observes that the Ministry has been allocated Rs. 2547.00 crore 
at RE 2019 -20 stage as against Rs.  3042.35 crore at B.E. 2019 -20 which is  a huge 
reduction of over 16%. The Committee observes that many of the projects/activities 
carried out by the Ministry of Culture, if postponed to a future date, will cause 
irreparable damage to the cultural heritge of our country. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may ensure that the available funds are 
utilized in an efficient manner, without rushing expenditure at the end of a Financial 
Year. 
14.  The Committee notes that the work carried out by Archaeological Survey of 
India, being seasonal in nature, can take place only after the monsoon season. The

initial quarters to the Ministry of Finance with due justification for not reducing the 
allocations of the Ministry at the RE stage in the light of the low expenditure figures 
of the Ministry till that quarter.

reduction of fund allocation at RE 2019 -20 and whether any provision ha s been 
made for the same at BE 2020-21.

construction of Pt. Deendayal Institute of Archa eology at Greater Noida. The 
Committee feels that there is  already a dearth of skilled manpower  in the 
Archaeology sector in India and timely completion of the Institute is directly linked

our ancient monu ments and tangible heritage. The Committee, therefore,

the project may be released at the earliest. The Ministry may seek additional funds 
for the completion of the project at RE 2020-21 stage.

37.  With regard to Adarsh monuments, the Ministry, in its written reply, has stated that

facilities are not available and upgrading existing facilities is a regular phenomenon 
undertaken by ASI. In the year 2018 -19 and 2019 -20, though no new monuments have 
been included as Adarsh monuments , 52 monuments have been selected for upgradation 
and providing amenities. 
38.  The Committee is of the view that the preservation of our cultural herita ge – 
both tangible and intangible – should be given its due importance since the damage 
caused to the same, due to the lack of funds or otherwise, is often irreversible in 
nature. The Committee,therefore, observes that maintenance of monuments cannot 
be postponed to a later date due to non-availability of funds. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may request the Government to allocate 
the revenue generated by ASI through sale of entry tickets and other sources, only 
for purpose of maintenance and preservation of the monuments. 
39.  The Committee is distressed to note that no new monument has been included in 
the Adarsh Monuments list in 2018-19 and 2019-20, though the Ministry has selected 
52 monuments for upgradation. The Committee has been given to understand  that 
budgetary constraints prevent ASI from selecting a higher number of monuments  
for upgradation and providing amenities . Given  the present pace, it would take 
decades to provide amenities at all the 3,691Centrally protected monuments.

41.  The Committee appreciates the e -ticketing initiative of the ASI  and desires that 
this initiative should be extended to all monuments at the earliest. 
42.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider bri nging out 
combined tickets  for tourists, both through e -ticketing and its physical counters. 
This would encourage the tourists to visit more ASI monuments without the hassle 
of having to individually book tickets for each site/monument.The Committee 
recommends that the ASI may extend its e -ticketing expertise to the ticketed 
monuments/sites protected by the State Governments. 

12

walls through Government agencies like WAPCOS, TCIL and NBCC. At present, 
boundary wall at 120 monuments ha ve been completed and is under progress at 160

44.  The Committee feels that encroachment is one of the serious issues faced in the 
preservation and conservation of monuments in our country. The Committee notes 
that b oundary wall has been completed or is under progress  at 280 monuments , 
which is meagre as compared to the total number of monuments (3 ,691) protected 
by ASI. The Committee recommends that ASI should conduct a survey of  the 
monuments under its protection  which require boundary wall  and assessthe 
budgetary requirements therefor.  
45.  The Committee desires that top priority should be given to excavation and 
conservation of ancient remains of the Stone Age. 
46.  The Committee emph asizes the need for greater co -ordination between ASI, 
State Governments and the local authorities in the matter of prevention and removal 
of encroachments at our monuments. The Committee recommends that strict 
punitive action should be taken, in coordination with the State Governments, against 
the encroachers.  
47.  The Committee also urges that the field offices of ASI should pursue such cases 
of encroachment persistently with the District Authorities on urgent basis and chalk 
a way out in such cases. The Committee also underlines the need for adequate follow 
up of the cases filed in Court of law against the encroachers.

the National Mission on Libraries for ad ministrative, logistic, planning and budgeting

ANTHROPOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA 
73.  Anthropological Survey of India (AnSI), a premier organization for Anthropological 
research under the Ministry of Culture, Government of India, was established in 1945 to 
document the biological and cultural diversity o f the people of India. The AnSI  has a 
presence through its Head Office located in Kolkata, seven Regional Centres, one Sub -
Regional Centre, a Camp Office, and one Permanent as well as three other Field Stations. 
It has been pursuing its mandate of mapping t he bio-cultural particularities and diversities 
for over seven decades and in the process has generated massive information on all the 
communities of India. The AnSI makes its presence felt to the wider world through its 
publications like half -yearly House  journal, Journal of the Anthropological Survey of 
India, quarterly Newsletter, Memoirs and occasional publications including the world 
wide web . Anthropological Survey of India is the one and only institution of its kind 
dedicatedto holistic study of the mankind with specialized man power in Cultural & 
Physical Anthropology, Human Ecology, Psychology, Biochemistry, Linguistics and 
Folklore. The organisation is working towards application of its technology based advance 
research in human development and wel fare. Documentation of bio -cultural heritage and 
regional/national databases and dissemination through published research work, national 
& international conferences, workshops, awareness programmes, audio -visual 
documentation and curation of exhibitions ar e activity evidences of inclusive approach of 
AnSI.

NATIONAL CULTURE FUND  
131. NCF's primary mandate is to establish and nurture Public Private Partnerships (PPP) 
in the field of Cultural heritage.   NCF's role is to catalyze relationships between private, 
public, government, non -government agencies, private institutions and foundatio ns and 
mobilize resources for the restoration, conservation, protection and development of 
India's rich tangible and intangible cultural heritage. The National Culture Fund is 
managed by a Council and an Executive Committee . The Council has a maximum 
strength of twenty four members, with a maximum of nineteen eminent members 
representing the corporate and public sector, private foundations and nonprofit 
organizations. The Hon‟ble Minister, Culture, is the Chairperson of the Council. The 
Executive Committee is chaired by the Secretary, Ministry of Culture. 

32 
 
132.  NCF receives proposals from reputed agencies like the Archaeological Survey 
of India and State archaeological departments for projects related to monuments, 
monasteries and  other historically important buildings that are in urgent need of 
conservation, but due to lack of funding, their upkeep and maintenance becomes difficult. 
These projects are then taken forward for partnership with various Donors for partnership 
under their CSR activities. The projects received by NCF are evaluated and recommended 
by NCF Sub Committee for Project Selection. NCF presents these projects to the 
Executive Committee of NCF for final approval. Once a project is approved by the 
Executive Committe e, the NCF team enters into detailed negotiations with the 
implementing agency, such as the scope of work, time -frame, deliverables, schedule of 
payments and the duration of the project and A Memorandum of Understanding is signed 
by the donor organization, NCF and the proposer/implementing agency.  
133.  Each project is managed independently by a Project Implementation 
Committee (PIC) that has due representation from the donor/ contributor/ co -
promoter/implementing agencies. The Project Implementation Committee has 
representation from NCF and whenever required civic authorities and the Archaeological 
Survey of India so that proper assessment of work can be done and fund can be released 
accordingly.  A separate joint Bank Account is maintained for each project tha t is 
operated by the representative of NCF and the Donor/Funding Agencies. Detailed 
accounts of each project are incorporated in the NCF Accounts which are audited by the 
Comptroller and Auditor General of Indiaannually. 
134. The Committee notes that the NCF An nual Report has not been 
published/updated on the website since 2014 -15. Similarly, the last completed 
projects was updated on the NCF website in 2017. The Committee observes that the 
website of the NCF being its gateway to potential donors, both individuals as well as 
organizations and therefore, the website should be updated to showcase its activities 
to the visitors in a transparent manner. 
135. The Committee feels that since National Culture Fund considers private/public 
institutions and individuals as equal partners of the Government in the management 
of the cultural heritage of India, efforts should be made by the Ministry to maintain 
transparency in the works executed under the scheme to lend them a sense of equal 
ownership and proper utilization of funds to the private/public institutions and 
individuals who contribute to the NCF account. The Committee  further 
recommends that the Ministry may proactively keep the donor 
organization/individual updated in this regard.

facades, drainage system etc.  After approval of the heritage bye -laws by the Authority, the same

Heritage Bye -Laws to facilitate the online ap plication system of NMA under „Ease of doing 
Business‟.

RE stage in 2020 -21, as against Rs. 89.14 crore at BE stage in 2020 -21. The 
Committee desires to know the activities which were hampered due to the reduction 
in allocation at RE stage in 2019-20. 
(Para 113 ) 
VACANCIES EXISTING IN VARIOUS ORGANIZATIONS OF THE MINISTRY 
 The Committee notes the high number of vacancies under National Library, 
Central Reference Library, Raja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation and other 
library institutes across the country. The Committee rec ommends that the Ministry 
may holistically examine the availability of skilled human resource in the field of 
library management and come up with long -term solutions to resolve the issue of 
vacancies. 
(Para 115) 
 The Committee is worried to note that aroun d one-third posts of the sanctioned 
strength are lying vacant in CCRT, Gandhi Smriti etc. The Committee takes serious 
note of the lack of adequate staff in majority of the Organizations under Ministry of 
Culture. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take concrete measures 
to fill the vacancies under its Organizations within a fixed timeframe and apprise 
the Committee of the progress made in this regard. 
(Para 116) 
The Committee takes special note of the vacancies existing in Archaeological Survey 
of India. The Committee desires to know the trend of existing vacancies in ASI for 
the last 5 years. The Committee finds that even the sanctioned staff strength of 8,426 
is not adequate given the number of monuments under the ambit of the 
organization. The  Committee, therefore, recommends that besides taking time -
bound action to fill the vacancies present in ASI, the Ministry should also undertake 
a review of the overall staff requirement of ASI. 
(Para 117) 
 The Committee may be apprised of the major findings of the Report and the 
action being taken by the Ministry thereon. Further, the Committee desires to be 
updated on the present status of the key posts at National Gallery of Modern Art. 
(Para 119) 
NATIONAL MISSION FOR PRESERVATION OF MANUSCRIPTS 
 The Committee is distressed to note the 55% vacancies in the National Mission 
for Manuscripts, which is one of the primary reasons behind the huge reduction in 
BE 2020 -21 allocation. The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for such a 
large number of posts lying vacant in NMM.  
(Para 125) 

52 
 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may ensure that the manuscripts 
digitized under NMM are routinely published online as well as in the form of books 
so as to give research scholars easy access to the same. Checks may be put in place to 
ensure that quality is not compromised in the digitization process of the 
manuscripts.  
(Para 126) 
CULTURAL MAPPING OF INDIA 
 The Committee is concerned to note that out of Rs. 42.78 crore allocated for 
Cultural Mapping in 2018 -19 and 2019 -20, a mere 2.74% i.e., Rs. 1.17 crore has 
been spent in these two years. The Committee failed to comprehend the reasons for 
the same. The Committee may be apprised of the steps being taken by the Ministry 
to strengthen the IT backbone for primary data collection in respect of B lock-level 
programmes as envisaged under the Mission, to produce a database of tangible as 
well as intangible cultural assets in the country. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to devise an effective action plan to resolve the 
institutional issues being faced in the execution of this project. 
(Para 130) 
NATIONAL CULTURE FUND  
 The Committee notes that the NCF Annual Report has not been 
published/updated on the website since 2014 -15. Similarly, the last completed 
projects was updated on the NC F website in 2017. The Committee observes that the 
website of the NCF being its gateway to potential donors, both individuals as well as 
organizations and therefore, the website should be updated to showcase its activities 
to the visitors in a transparent manner. 
(Para 134) 
 The Committee feels that since National Culture Fund considers private/public 
institutions and individuals as equal partners of the Government in the management 
of the cultural heritage of India, efforts should be made by the Ministry t o maintain 
transparency in the works executed under the scheme to lend them a sense of equal 
ownership and proper utilization of funds to the private/public institutions and 
individuals who contribute to the NCF account. The Committee further 
recommends th at the Ministry may proactively keep the donor 
organization/individual updated in this regard. 
(Para 135) 
KALA SANSKRITI VIKAS YOJANA 
 The Committee takes strong note of the extremely slow pace of expenditure 
under the Revenue Head of allocation for Kala Sanskriti Vikas Yojana scheme. Only 
65.77% of the funds allocated under Revenue head in RE 2019 -20 have been utilized 
up to January, 202 0.  Compared to BE 2019 -20 allocation of Rs. 227.74 crore under 

53 
 
Revenue Head, the expenditure is a mere 45.7%. The Committee is of the view that 
the drastic reduction under Revenue head of this scheme at RE 2019 -20 is only 
because of poor expenditure patte rn. Even after the cut, the Ministry has failed to 
utilize the amount that was granted at RE 2019 -20 stage. The Committee may be 
apprised of the reasons which led to the sheer underutilization of funds under this 
scheme. The Committee recommends that the M inistry may endeavor to make 
optimal utilization of the amount that has been allocated at BE stage in 2020-21. 
(Para 138) 
ARTISTS PENSION SCHEME AND WELFARE FUND 
 The Committee is unhappy to note that the fund allocation under the ‘Artists 
Pension Scheme and Welfare Fund’ has decreased from Rs. 23.40 crore at RE 2018 -
19 to Rs. 21.15 crore at RE 2019 -20. The Committee observes that Rs. 19.73 crore 
expenditure incurred on providing pension to 4120 beneficiaries in 2018 -19 amounts 
to a pension of about Rs. 400 0 per month which is a paltry sum considering the fact 
that many artists have no source of income in old age to meet their basic 
requirements. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may review 
the pension amount granted to beneficiaries on annual basis in the light of inflation 
and rising living expenses. 
(Para 142) 
 The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for which the number of 
beneficiaries of this scheme has come down from 4120 in 2018 -19 to 3133 in 2020 -21 
(till January, 2020). The Committee feels that even the figure of 4120 beneficiaries is 
quite low, given the vastness of our country. Obviously instead of covering more 
beneficiaries, the Ministry seems to be going in the reverse direction. 
(Para 143) 
The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Ministry to ensure timely 
disbursal of the Artistes Pension. 
(Para 146) 
The Committee desires to know the reasons for not holding even a single meeting 
to process the applications in 2015 -16 and 2016 -17. The Committee feels that t he 
Ministry cannot afford to keep artistes’ applications for pension, pending for years. 
The Ministry should ensure that regular meetings are held to update the list of 
beneficiaries entitled for pension under the scheme of the Ministry. 
(Para 148) 
 The Committee further notes that no artist belonging to 10 out of the 28 States 
for which details have been provided, has been added as a beneficiary of the Artistes 
Pension Scheme of the Ministry in the past 4 years. The Committee may be apprised 
of the actions taken by the Ministry to create awareness about this Scheme in these 
States. The Committee feels that there is a pressing need to reach out to artistes, 
especially in under -represented States so that there is equitable representation of 
artistes rec eiving funds under the Scheme. The Committee recommends that the 

54 
 
Ministry may take concrete steps to cover more artistes from under -represented 
States. 
(Para 149) 
INITIATIVES TO REACH OUT TO THE YOUTH 
The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Ministry to reach out to the 
youth in order to preserve intangible cultural heritage of our country. The 
Committee recommends special focus in this regard for which the Ministry may 
make efficient use of social media to build a connection with the tech -savvy young 
generation. 
(Para 151) 
NORTH-EASTERN AREAS 
 The Committee is constrained to note the low expenditure pattern in 2018 -19 
and 2019-20 which implies that the Ministry is not paying enough attention to the 
North-Eastern Region in its projects and sche mes. The Committee desires to know 
how the Ministry plans to carry out its schemes/projects in the NER with the highly 
reduced allocation of Rs. 57.80 crore at BE stage in 2020 -21, as against the BE 2019-
20 allocation of Rs. 175.50 crore. 
(Para 154) 
NATIONAL MONUMENTS AUTHORITY 
 The Committee may be apprised about the average time taken by NMA to 
dispose an application seeking permission for construction in prohibited and/or 
regulated area of a Centrally protected monument. The Committee desires to kn ow 
whether there is a mechanism in place to monitor whether any unpermitted 
construction takes place in the prohibited and regulated area of a monument. 
(Para 158) 
 The Committee recommends that NMA may, in partnership with any online 
mapping platform, pub lish maps showing the exact boundaries of prohibited and 
regulated areas for each of the 3,691 Centrally protected monuments. This would 
clear the confusion existing among many people regarding whether they need to 
apply for permission for carrying out con struction activities in the vicinity of 
protected monuments. 
(Para 159) 
 The Committee further recommends that NMA may, in coordination with ASI, 
create awareness among people living in the vicinity of monuments about the 
restrictions on construction. The procedure for applying for permission of 
construction in these areas may also be communicated to the local populace. 
(Para 160) 
The Committee takes serious note of the sluggish pace of finalization and laying 
of Heritage Bye-laws for the Centrally protecte d monuments. The Committee notes 

55 
 
that only 5 HBLs covering 31 Centrally protected monuments have so far been laid 
before both the Houses of the Parliament since the NMA came into existence in 
2011. The Committee desires to know the time by which NMA would finalize the 
HBLs for all the 3,691 Centrally protected monuments. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the NMA may come up with an effective plan of action to draft 
and finalize the HBLs for all monuments across the country.  
(Para 161) 
NEED FOR BETTER CO-ORDINATION WITH MINISTRIES AND STATE 
GOVERNMENTS 
The Committee appreciates the financial support being provided by National 
Culture Fund for this upcoming project. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry/ASI may extend their expertise in Museums to M inistry of Shipping in 
setting up the National Maritime Museum at Lothal.  
(Para 163) 
The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by ASI, in this regard.  
(Para 164) 
 The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministries of Civil Aviation, Shipping, 
Road Transport & Highways, Culture, Tourism, Railways  are not only inter -
related and interconnected but also have a common objective to improve 
connectivity and better amenities for the benefit of tourists, travellers and faster 
movement of freight within the country. The Committee, therefore, feels that there 
is a pressing need for having an effective co -ordination mechanism among these 
Ministries so that the policies and guidelines being formulated by them are executed 
seamlessly and can supplement each other in achieving these objectives. This will not 
only increase effectiveness and efficiency, but will also help in utilization of funds 
and skilled manpower to the maximum possible extent. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that an easy -to-use interface shou ld be made available which allows 
hassle-free communication and co -ordination amongst them. A hotline number 
which is common to all these Ministries, may be established so that whenever 
emergency arises, there can be effective and prompt coordination among  these 
Ministries and issues in hand can be resolved at the earliest. 
(Para 165) 
MISCELLANEOUS 
Indian Institute of Heritage and Conservation  
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may set up the Indian Institute of 
Heritage and Conservation on priority, to meet the shortage of skilled manpower in 
several Organizations under its domain. 
(Para 167) 

56 
 
Development of Archaeological Sites 
 The Committee is pleased to note the budget announcement made on the 
proposed development of the 5 archaeological sites as iconic sites with on -site 
museums. The Committee hopes that the development work at these sites is carried 
out in a time-bound manner and more sites across the country may be identified and 
selected for development in the future. The Committee rec ommends that the 
Ministry may ensure strict adherence of effective safeguards so as to ensure that the 
developmental work at these sites do not hamper any future excavation activities 
there. 
(Para 170) 
Cellular Jail in Port Blair 
 The Committee may be apprised of the response received from the Andaman 
and Nicobar Administration in this regard. The Committee feels that ASI has the 
expertise required in such matters and recommends that ASI may extend its 
assistance to A&N Administration in preparation of the nomination dossier for 
inclusion of Cellular Jail in the UNESCO World Heritage list. 
(Para 172) 
Asiatic Society, Mumbai 
 The Committee would like to know the present status of implementation of the 
recommendations made in the Report of the Review Committee. 
(Para 174) 
 The Committee observes that the Seventh Pay Commission is yet to be 
implemented in ASM. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should look 
into the financial and manpower requirements of the ASM and take urgent steps to 
implement the Seventh Pay Commission in therein. The Committee desires that the 
Ministry should take proactive steps to declare the Asiatic Society of Mumbai as an 
Institute of National Importance without affecting its autonomy. 
(Para 175) 
Zonal Cultural Centres   
 
 The Committee observes that substantial amount of funds are being given to 
Zonal Cultural Centres. However, the output is not commensurate with the 
magnitude of funding. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be 
a robust monitoring mechanism for assessment of Zonal Cultural Centres.   
(Para 176)

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
    Road Transport is a critical component of the infrastructure required for the economic 
development of a country. Its impact on the pace, structure and pattern of development can be 
gauged by the fact that road transport is estimated to handle 90 percent and 69 percent of the 
countrywide passenger and freight traffic respectively, as per the National Transport 
Development Policy Committee Report of 2011 -12. High growth and proper maintenance of 
the road network in India is a significant pre -requisite for her aspirations to become a $5 
trillion economy by 2024-25. 
2. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways shoulders the responsibil ities and 
tasks pertaining to , inter alia , construction and maintenance of National Highways (NHs); 
administration of the National Highways Act,1956; National Highways Authority of India 
Act, 1988; National Highways Fee (Determination of Rates and Collection) Rules, 2008; 
Motor Vehicles Act 1988;  and Central Motor Vehicles Rules 1989, as also formulation of 
broad policies relating to road transport and automotive norms, besides making arrangements 
for movement of vehicular traffic with neighbouring countries. 
3. India has the second largest road network in the world, at about 58.98 lakh kilometers. 
This comprises National Highways, Expressways, State Highways, Major District Roads, 
Other District Roads and Village Roads as under: 
National Highways 1,32,500 km 
State Highways 1,56,694 km 
Other Roads 56,08,477 km 
Total 58,97,671 km 
 
4. The various associated offices under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways 
are as follows:  
i. National Highways Authority of India (NHAI):   
Set up through an Act of Parliament in 1988, NHAI is responsible for the 
development, maintenance and management of the National Highways entrusted to it 
and for matters related or incidental there to. The NHAI became operational in 
February, 1995. 
ii. National Highways & Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. (NHIDCL) : 
NHIDCL is  responsible for the construction/ up -grading/widening of National 
Highways in parts of the country which share international boundaries with 
neighbouring countries in order to promote regional connectively on a sustainable 
basis. 

2 
 
iii. Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE):  
IAHE is a collaborative body which was set up in the year 1983 with the objective of 
fulfilling the long felt need for training of Highway Engineers in the country, both at 
the entry level and during their service period. 
iv. Indian Road Congress (IRC):  
The IRC was formally registered as a Society on 24 th September 1937 under the 
Societies Registration Act of 1860 for periodical holding of road conferences to 
discuss issues related to road construction, maintenance & development. 
ANNUAL PLAN 2019-20    
5. The Ministry, in its written reply, has informed that it had projected a total GBS 
requirement of Rs. 1,26,772.97 crore under RE 2019 -20. The proposed allocations under RE 
2019-20 is Rs. 83,015.97 crore, i.e. same as that of the BE 2019 -20 outlay. The Ministry 
further stated that NHAI has been authorized to raise Internal & Extra Budgetary Resources 
(IEBR) to the tune  of Rs. 75,000 crore. With regard to any projects/programmes of the 
Ministry getting affected because of the shortfall in actual allocation vis-à-vis the projected 
demand of the Ministry, it informed that the shortfall would affect ongoing projects under  
National Highways (Original) [NH(O)] scheme. However, considering that BE 2020-21 shall 
be fully available with effect from 01.04.2020, major shortfall was not anticipated.

7. The Committee notes with concern the slow pattern of utilization as only 75% of 
funds could be spent till 31 st January, 2020 . Even the amount allocated at R.E. stage 
could not be spent under some of the heads , except National Highways (Original). The 
Committee feels that there is laxity on the part of the Ministry in releasing funds for 
other schemes . In fact,  it is only focusing on construction of new highways, whereas  
important heads like Maintenance and Repair, Road Transport and Road Safety, 
Research and Development , received paltry amounts in comparison to the size of our 
highways network. The Committee is of the considered view that h aphazard spending 
towards the end of the Financial Year is bound to cause quality issues in respect of the 
projects carried out under these Heads. 
8. The Ministry, in its written reply, has cited the following  reasons for less spending: -
  
(i) Externally Aided Projects – There is delay in some Projects being executed with 
loan assistance from JICA, ADB and World Bank. Accordingly, physical and 
financial targets could not be achieved.  
(ii) Poor tender response , delay in award of new projects, poor pr ogress/ cash flow 
problems of contractors, termination of contracts, delay in land acquisition  have 
restricted the utilization of funds for projects in North East Region. 
(iii) Poor progress of works, law and order problems  are the reasons for less 
spending in development of Roads in LWE affected areas. 
(iv) Delay in receipt of Utilization Certificates (UCs) from States for release of 
funds for development of State Roads under CRIF Scheme. 
(v) Slow progress in bus port scheme as most of the projects are at DPR stage.  
(vi) Few projects sanctioned under IDTR and I&C scheme and non -submission of 
UCs by States for existing projects.  
9.   The Committee finds the reasons too routine in nature. The Committee

Excessive spending in the last quarter is against the cannons of fiscal accounting.

(i) Proposals for re -appropriation of funds under Second Supplementary 
Demands for Grants for 2019 -20 have been duly submitted considering 
progress of projects/ schemes, estimated expenditures, etc., towards ensuring 
utilization of balance funds. 
(ii) Actions have been initiated towards release of funds for State Roads under

limit of available unspent balance of such State(s) of previous years‟.

ROAD DEVELOPMENT 
35.   The Ministry  has been entrusted with the responsibility of development of Road 
Transport and Highways in general and construction & maintenance of National 
Highways (NHs) in particular. All roads other than National Highways in the States fall 
within the jurisdiction of respective State Governments. In order to assist the State 
Governments in the development of State roads, Central Government also provides 
financial assistance out of the Central Road Fund (CRF) and Inter State Connectivity and 
Economic Importance (ISC & EI) scheme. Besides National Highways development 
Project (NHDP) & National Highway Interconnectivity Improvement programme 
(NHIIP), Ministry is implementing SARDP -NE & LWE schemes which includes 
National Highways and State roads. The Ministry is also re sponsible for evolving 
standards and specifications for roads and bridges in the country besides acting as a 
repository of technical information on roads and bridges. The length of National 
Highways for which the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, Government of India is 
responsible is 1,32,500 km. 
36.   The Ministry has further submitted that the National Highways system suffers from 
capacity constraints, inadequate pavement crust, poor geometrics and lack of safety 
features. Improvement of National Highways is undertaken by way of widening and 
strengthening of existing highways, reconstruction / widening of bridges and construction 
of bypasses after prioritizing the works within available resources. 
37.   The Committee takes into account  the deficiencies pointed out by  the Ministry. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should lay greater focus on  Research 

14 
 
and Development so as to improve poor road geometrics and road safety in its future 
projects. 
38.   The Committee notes that there are serious issues with regard to monitoring the 
quality of the road development projects carried out by the Ministry. The 
Committee would like  the Ministry to conduct a quality audit of its projects for  
effective quality checks in both construction and maintenance  of the pr ojects. The 
Committee recommends that adequate fund may be allocated for periodic quality 
checks over different stretches of a road under construction and/or maintenance , 
during various phases of the project, and also after its completion.  
39.   The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should chalk out a road 
quality score mechanism which can be  updated through out the various stages of 
progress of a road project. This score should be based on the quality of construction 
material, compliance with safety standards and user feedback. This score would also 
help in assessing the amount of funds needed to carry out repair works on the road – 
with roads needing less maintenance getting higher scores. The scoring of road 
projects should be linked to road contractor‟s portfolio and priority in awarding a 
road project be given to those contractors with a history of constructing quality road 
projects. 
40.   The Committee observes that inputs from stakeholders can help in preparation 
of DPRs to avoid post-construction issues. 
41.   The Committee is of the view that the efficiency of Highway alignment in 
Greenfield projects is much higher than Brownfield projects. The Committee 
recommends that as per the policy of MoRTH , linear road construction and 
Greenfield projects should be accorded utmost priority for construction of road 
projects. 
42.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure the inclusion of 
provision for service roads on both sides across the National Highways network. The 
Committee feels that important roads with significant traffic load, such as 
Hyderabad-Kurnool Tollgate to Bengaluru Route Tollgate and other such toll gates, 
should be given priority. The Committee feels that this would allow smooth passage 
of city traffic as well as slow  speed vehicles and lower the number of road accidents 
happening on the National Highways. 
MAINTENANCE AND REPAIR OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS 
43.   The Ministry has informed that v arious types of M&R works undertaken on NHs are 
Ordinary Repairs (OR, involving routine maintenance, such as maintenance of culverts, 
patch/ pot -hole repairs, crack seal ing, roadside drainage, repairing of shoulders, etc.), 
Periodic Renewals (PR, i.e. provision of renewal coat to the wearing surface at a 
predetermined frequency), Special Repairs (SR, which are urgent works of original 

15 
 
nature, such as repairs to culverts, bridges, etc.) and Emergent/ Flood Damage Repairs 
(FDRs, i.e. immediate repairs to roads affected by heavy rains/ flood, cyclone, landslides, 
sand dunes, etc. to restore traffic). These works are taken up as per available resources  
and inter-se priority of works to keep the NHs in traffic worthiness.  The M&R of NH 
stretches are carried out for the stretches not covered under any programme or completed 
stretches where there are no liabilities of contractors to maintain such stretches.   
44.   For the NH stretch es developed on EPC mode (Engineering, Procurement, 
Construction), the contractor is responsible for remedying the defects and concurrent 
maintenance of project highway during the four years defect liability period after 
completion of the work. For NH stre tches developed on BOT mode/ HAM, the 
Concessionaire is responsible for the maintenance of the project highway during the 
concession period. For some of the developed NH stretches through public funding, 
maintenance contracts have been taken up for a defin ite time period (4 to 9 years) on 
Operate, Maintenance and Transfer (OMT) basis. The maintenance of the project 
highway under OMT contracts is the responsibility of the concessionaire. 
45.   With regard to the maintenance of National Highways, the allocations that are 
available annually for M&R of NHs are of the order of about 40% of the actual 
requirements as per the Ministry‟s stipulated norms based on the Report of the Committee 
(2001) (i.e. available allocations are of the order of about Rs. 2,520 crore as against the 
estimated fund requirement of Rs. 5,000 crore as per the Ministry‟s Norms for 
Maintenance of NHs).   
46.   The Committee strongly recommends that a mechanism should be established to 
periodically monitor the quality of Highways. A policy framework should be set in 
place to ensure that repair  works and maintenance of Highways are carried out  
within a prescribed timeframe so as to ensure certain minimum standards of 
pliability on the Highways. 
47.   The Ministry has informed the Committee that against RE 2019-20 projected demand 
of Rs. 4,100 crore  for Maintenance & Repair of NHs including Swachhta Activities , 
funds to the tune of Rs. 2,100 crore were actually proposed at RE 2019 -20 stage. There 
was a projected demand of Rs. 5,100 crore for Maintenance &  Repair of NHs including 
Swachhta Activities for the year 2020 -21 against which the outlay proposed is Rs. 2,600 
crore. Surprisingly, the Ministry has informed that t he outlay proposed for Maintenance 
& Repair of NHs including Swachhta Activities at BE 202 0-21 are sufficient at this stage  
and additional requirements, if any, shall be appropriately proposed at RE stage. 
48.   The Committee fails to understand how the Ministry terms the outlay proposed 
for Maintenance & Repair of NHs to be sufficient at this stag e when the outlay has 
been reduced to half of the projected amount. The Committee feels that even the Rs. 
5,100 crore demand, which comes to merely 3.3% of the Ministry‟s overall projected 
demand at BE stage in 2020 -21, is grossly inadequate to meet the ma intenance 
requirements of the vast National Highways network in India, which continues to be 

16 
 
ill-maintained and riddled with pot-holes and other maintenance issues. 
49.   The Ministry has submitted that it is taking up the monetisation of the completed NHs 
stretches on Toll -Operate-Transfer (TOT) model to generate funds.  In projects under 
Operation and Maintenance (O&M), the Concessionaire / contractor is required to follow 
the relevant specifications with clearly laid down timelines for different activities e.g. 
filling of pots, repairing the shoulders etc.    
50.   So far as minimizing financial liability of the Govt. for M&R activities is concerned, 
the inter-se priority for carrying out Maintenance and Repai r (M&R) of NHs generally 
depends upon nature and extent of damages, overall condition of NH stretches, traffic 
density, minimum works required to be undertaken to ensure traffic worthiness of NHs, 
status of action taken up for new developmental works, avai lability of funds, etc. The NH 
stretches under Defect Liability Period (DLP) obligation or stretches under Build, Operate 
and Transfer (BOT)/ Hybrid Annuity Mode l (HAM)/ Operate, Maintenance and Transfer 
(OMT) Concessions, ongoing works on NHs are responsi bility of the respective

Monetisation of Assets through Toll-Operate-Transfer (TOT) Model:  
65.   The Ministry has conceptualised an innovative way for raising funds through 
Monetisation of completed Road Assets  under Toll-Operate-Transfer (TOT) Model. The 
scheme envisages bidding of bundled nati onal highways for a concession period of 30 
years. The first bundle comprised of 9 projects, totalling 681 km of roads in Andhra 
Pradesh and Gujarat. It was awarded in 2018 to Macquarie for Rs. 9,681 Crore, which 
was about 1.5 times the NHAI's estimates. T he second bundle comprising over 586 kms 
spread over four States – Rajasthan, Gujarat, West Bengal and Bihar was also placed in 
the market which was, however,  restructured thereafter. The third bundle compris ing 9 
projects totalling 566.27 km of road in Ut tar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and Tamil Nadu , 
was awarded in November 2019 to M/s. Cube Mobility Investment Fund Pvt. Ltd , for 
which the Concession Agreement was also signed on 27.12.2019 with 9 SPVs. The bid 
for fourth bundle of TOT comprises of 6 projects, totaling 341.58 km length of roads in 
the States of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, MP & UT of J&K was recently invited with Bid 
due date of 13.02.2020. The Cabinet has given its approval to the amendments proposed 
in the TOT Model  and henceforth, Public fu nded National Highway projects which are 
operational and have toll revenue generation history of one year after the Commercial 
Operations Date can be monetized through the TOT Model. Under this, the right of 
collection of Toll Fees for operational public -funded NH projects is to be assigned for a 

21 
 
pre-determined period to the Concessionaires (developers/ investors) against upfront 
payment of a lump -sum amount. O&M obligations of such projects would rest with the 
Concessionaires until the completion of the pe riod under TOT Model. The CCEA has 
also given approval to NHAI for raising funds from banks through securitization of user 
fees.

2,165.77 Crore is expected by February and the third Bundle (TOT-5) for Rs. 2,800 Crore 
is also expected to be called within this financial year.

84.    The Ministry, in its written reply to a query regarding its plans to repay the

funds through InvIt (Investment Infrastructure Trust) after approval of CCEA.

been given the mandate to set up an InvIT to monetize its completed stretches of public 
funded national highways with the objective of mobilizing additional resources  through 
capital markets. NHAI will be able to securitise future cash inflows through an InvIT, as 
it allows the organisation to monetize illiquid and stable cash generating infrastructure 
assets. It will attract long-term capital, allowing the investors to have an indirect exposure 
in the project(s). This proposition is more attractive for foreign investors, which are 
hesitant to take direct exposure in highway projects. Intermediaries for NHAI InvIT are 
being appointed. Identification of project stretches  for placing under NHAI InvIT, is 
under process. As per the approved timelines, InvIT may go for issue in May, 2020.

WORK FINANCED FROM PERMANENT BRIDGE FEE FUND (PBFF) 
179. The Committee sought information from the Ministry on whether  BE 2020-21 
allocation of Rs. 18.32 crores under the head „Work Financed from PBFF‟  will be 
sufficient, since the BE allocation in 2019 -20 was Rs. 50 crores . The Ministry, in its 
written reply, has informed that t he fund is State specific. This fund is actual toll 
collection on NHs entrusted to State Governments.  The fund collected on N Hs by a State 
is re-allocated to concerned States for NHs works in that State.  The fund is non -lapsable. 
Rs. 50 crore was earmarked under BE 2019 -20 comprising of Rs. 39.54 crore from 
unspent balance of previous years‟ allocations and Rs. 10.46 crore coll ection during 
2017-18.  Collection has reduced since 2016 -17 because of the policy decision taken by 
the Ministry to exempt tolling of projects costing less than Rs. 100 crore vide circular no. 
H-25016/01/2014-(Toll) Vol.2 -Part/130 dated 09.09.2016. Consid ering the progress of 
projects under the scheme and also since no new projects have been sanctioned under the 
scheme, the outlay under the scheme is proposed to be reduced to Rs.  10 crore at RE 
stage. For the next financial year 2020 -21, a provision of Rs.  18.32 crore has been made 
which is actual toll collection for the year 2018-19. 
180. The Committee hopes that the reduction in toll collection caused by the policy 
decision of the Ministry exempting tolling of projects costing less than Rs. 100 crore 
will not cause shortfall in the funding of NH works of the concerned States. The 
Committee recommends that the shortfall faced, if any, by the State Governments 

54 
 
because of the policy decision, may be taken care of by the Ministry so as to avoid 
any delays in the ongoing projects under PBFF.

210.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministries  of Civil Aviation, Shipping,

connectivity and better amenities for the benefit of tourists, travellers and fas ter 
movement of freight within the country. The Committee, therefore, feels that there

Ministries so that the policies and guidelines being formulated by them are executed 

61

which is common to all these Ministries, may be established so that whenever 
emergency arises, there can be effe ctive and prompt coordination among these 
Ministries and issues in hand can be resolved at the earliest. 
EARMARKING OF OBLIGATED ALLOCATIONS FOR SCHEDULED CASTE SUB 
PLAN (SCSP) AND TRIBAL SUB PLAN (TSP) 
211.  The Ministry, in its written reply, informed the Committee that although the Ministry 
has been earmarking 4.3% of Annual Capital Outlay under TSP component wherein specific 
NH/road projects are being developed which are fully confined within one or more t ribal 
districts, it is not feasible to adopt this approach for dedicated earmarking of funds under 
SCSP component as either development of NHs nor earmarking of funds for NH projects is 
feasible to specifically benefit any specific category/community. The Ministry has further 
stated that in case of NH projects, which are linear in nature, it is not feasible to objectively 
monitor the beneficiaries especially on the basis of demographical distribution, although 
development of many NH stretches passing through areas dominantly inhabited by Scheduled 
Tribes (ST) / Scheduled Castes (SC) eventually benefit such areas towards ushering in overall 
socio-economic development. Accordingly, the Ministry has requested NITI Aayog, 
Department of Economic Affairs and Minis try of Social Justice & Empowerment from time 
to time to exempt the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways from mandatory earmarking 
of funds under SCSP as is allowed for Ministry of Railways, which is also a similar type of 
linear infrastructure development network distributed in the country. 
212. The Committee agrees with the Ministry‟s view that monitoring the beneficiaries 
especially on demographical distribution is not feasible in case of linear projects like 
National Highways. The Committee recommends tha t NITI Aayog may consider the 
request of the Ministry with regard to seeking exemption from mandatory earmarking 
of funds under SCSP. The Committee desires that the Ministry may furnish the  
updated status regarding the request it made to NITI Aayog.

Curbing excessive usage of horns 
219. The Ministry has issued G.S.R. 953(E) dated 05.10.2016 vide which amendment has 
been made in Form 22 of the Central Motor vehicle Rules, 1989 to add the noise le vels of 
the vehicles.  
220. As per rule 119 of Central Motor vehicle Rules, 1989, no motor vehicle, including 
agricultural tractor and combine harvester, shall be fitted with any multi -toned horn 
giving a succession of different notes or with any other sound pr oducing device giving an 
unduly harsh, shrill, loud or alarming noise. The Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways, vide letter dated 12th June, 2017 and 11th August, 2017 has issued an 
advisory to all the State Governments and Union Territories to strictl y follow the 
provisions of Rule 119 of Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 regarding multi toned 
horns.  

64 
 
221. Furthermore, in rule no. 120(2) of Central Motor vehicle Rules, 1989 it is mentioned 
that every motor vehicle shall be constructed and maintained so as to conform to noise 
standards specified in Part E of the Schedule VI to the Environment (Protection) Rules, 
1986. 
222. Implementation of the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 and Central Motor vehicle 
Regulation, 1989 rests with the concerned States/ Union Territories. 
223. The Committee feels that the average Indian road user is habitua ted to honking 
excessively which in turn  contributes a lot to the noise pollution in big cities. 
Further, the Committee notes that the rules and laws are in place regarding fitting 
of loud hor ns on vehicles , but the same are not being implemented effectively. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may run promotional campaigns , 
especially on social media to promote responsible usage of horns. The same idea may 
also be advocated through the Driver Training Center Programme of the Ministry.

higher authorities.
