4.1. Due to various initiatives taken up under the aegis of ease of doing business and doing

AVERAGE OUTPUT SHIP BERTHDAY 
Recommendation/Observation  
5. On comparison of the above figures of 2019 -20 with data of 2018 -19, it has been 
noticed that t here was improvement only in 6 P orts viz., Haldia , Visakhapatnam, Cochin, 
Mormugao, Mumbai and JNPT.  However, in Ports of Kolkata, Paradip, Kamarajar, 
Chennai, V.O. Chidambaranar, New Mangalore and Deendayal, the average Output Per 
Ship Berthday is even less than that of 2018 -19. The Committee desires t hat the Ministry 
should look into the reasons for the decrease in average Output Per Ship Berthday of 7 Ports 
mentioned above and take remedial measures.                   (Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1. The reasons for the decrease in average Output Per Ship Berthday and reme dial 
measures suggested by the Ports are given as under: 
Kolkata: 
(i) Decrease was primarily due to increase in percentage of Non -Working Time, 
which was owing to non-Port account reasons. 
(ii) Poor performance of the handling contractor i n terms of poor equipment 
availability with regard to MHC, RST and TT  led to decrease in average ship -day 
output of container vessels  which in turn affected the overall average Ship -day 
Output. 
(iii) Also, due to Covid -19 impact, both Container import and export generation were 
adversely affected leading to lower output. 
Remedial measures by Port: 
(a) Mechanization of 3 NSD Berth - Converting the berth from non -MHC berth 
(where geared vessels used to be handled) to MHC berth (where gearless vessels 
may be handled). 

5 
 
(b) Introduction of Fixed Window Berthing (FWB):  Two FWBs per week introduced 
w.e.f. 23.09.2019 and the third window became operational from 29.11.2019. 
Paradip: 
OSBD of Liquid Bulk Vessels has been reduced from 52119 MT to 50544 in 2019 -20, which 
has affected the Gross productivity of the Port.  The reduction in average parcel size of the 
vessels resulted in slow discharge rate of the Cargo and thus OSBD of POL is affected. 
Kamarajar: 
(i) At Coal Berth 1, the conveyor system connecting Coal berth and NCTPS stack  
yard is frequently got breakdown due to old age structures and also Belt damages. 
Due to this, the berth stay of the vessels has been increased considerably which in 
turn affects the berth productivity. 
(ii) At Coal Berth 2, the pipe conveyor system of NTECL r uns 4.4 Km along the 
coastline which is getting frequent breakdown. Due to the corrosion effects, the 
pipe conveyor gantries in the conveyor system need to be replaced and the same is 
carried out by NTECL. NTECL informed that it is expected to complete by 
September 2020. Due to this, the berth productivity of Coal Berth 2 has been 
reduced considerably. 
Remedial measures by Port: 
(a) KPL is continuously pursuing with TANGEDCO for the replacement of conveyor 
belts at NCTPS plant in order to improve the performance of Coal Berth 1. 
(b) KPL is continuously pursuing with NTECL for the completion of all the pipe 
conveyor gantry replacement works in order to improve the performance of Coal 
Berth 2 
Chennai: 
(i) Increased number of less productive Project Cargo vessels  & 
other General Cargo vessels; and 
(ii) Decreased number of high productive dry bulk cargoes like Limestone/Dolomite 
vessels and Container vessels  for the year 2019 -20 when compared to 2018 -19. 
The shortfall was only in dry bulk wherein, the output per ship berthday decreased 
due to less number  of limestone / dolomite vessels ( viz., 47 vessels during 2018 -
19 as against  13 vessels during 2019 -20) which are normally handled by mobile 
harbour cranes with higher productivity. 
Remedial measures by Port: 
(a) The increase in draft level to 14 metres at JD2 berth at  Chennai port has attracted 
a Limestone Vessel of all -time high of 76342MT and a Gypsum vessel of 61600 

6 
 
MT during the month of March 2020 and  more such vessels are anticipated 
regularly, which will increase the volume and hence the productivity. 
V.O. Chidambaranar: 
     Increase in less productive cargoes like Machinery, Wind Mill Blade and Project 
Cargoes by 44.64% from 57,412 tonnes in 20l8 -19 to 83.042 tonnes in 2019 -20. 
Also, there was increase in shifting of deep draft vessels from the only 
multipurpose deep draft mechanized berth (IX Berth) which affects the 
productivity. 
Remedial measures by Port: 
(i) Port has constructed NCBIII berth with a proposal to add one more deep draft 
berth to handle multipurpose cargo vessels. However, dredging proposal is 
pending for approval from the Ministry. On addition of one more deep draft berth, 
increase in shifting of deep draft vessels can be avoided which would avoid pre-
Berthing Detention, reduced TRT and improve o verall average output per ship 
berthday. 
(ii) Incentive/ Penalty based on berthing norms reviewed to improve the productivity 
of the vessels at Berth. 
New Mangalore: 
(i) Less Crude Oil Handling at the SBM facility.  Crude oil imports declined due to 
shut down of some units by MRPL during April, May, Augu st and September, 
2019 due to up gradation to Bharat  VI standards, water scarcity, l andslides and 
also three weeks of non -working days on account of cyclonic weather in the 
month of September, 2019. 
(ii) Lower Output of Semi-Mechanized Dry bulk cargo due to Weather Constraint.  In 
the year 2019 -20, the Monsoon extended till October, causing constraints on the 
handling of Dry Bulk cargo such as iron ore fines, coal, urea, limestone etc. which 
resulted in a lower average output per ship berthday.  
Remedial measures by Port: 
(i) The operationalization of the m echanized coal handling facility at berth n o. 16 
will ensure higher output for all types of coal cargo during 2020-21. 
(ii) The port is teaming up with the captive Clients such as MRPL to e nsure smooth 
operations in the year 2020 -21.  The port is in close coordination with the captive 
users to not only handle higher cargo but also to increase the performance of its 
operations.  
Deendayal: 

7 
 
(i) Owing to implementation of the barrier in height for cargo dumping & storage, the 
feeding of cargo from hook point to the storage point & vice-versa, has slowed 
down significantly and this has in turn affected (reduced) the unloading / loading 
rates and the per berthday output for dry cargoes, especially bulk cargoes like coal 
etc. 
(ii) Cyclone warning: The Non weather working day was issued for  4 days (from 11 th 
to 14th June, 2019) at Kandla and for 3 days at Vadinar. At Kandla, this affected 
the normal cargo handling operations for nearly 5 days. 
(iii) Impact of COVID 19 pandemic :  The gradual spread of pandemic and the impact 
on cargo handling operations on account of th e subsequent lockdown from 22 nd 
March, 2020. Also due to problems in adequate supply of labour  for cargo 
handling and for carrying out loading / unloading operations caused significant 
impact in decreasing the output of bulk cargoes handled at the port.

SETHUSAMUDRAM CORPORATION LIMITED 
Recommendation/Observation  
9. The Committee observes that this project is a vital link to Gulf region which is a very 
productive corridor from India’s economic point of view. The Committee would, therefore, 
like the Ministry to take all possible steps to expedite adjudication in the matter.  (Para 65) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1. The Sethusamudram Corporation Limited (SCL) was created as special purpose 
vehicle vide, Cabinet decision dated 02.09.2004 for raising finance and to undertake activities 
for creation /  operation of a navigable channel connecting Gulf of Mannar to Bay of  
Bengal.  On 19.05.2005, CCEA approved the Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project (SSCP) 
passing through Ram Sethu / Adam’s Bridge (Ali gnment No. 6).  While the said p roject was 
under implementation, due to a large number of court c ases, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India 
ordered on 31.08.2007 and 14.09.2007  to stop dr edging in Adam’s Bridge area.   There has 
been no dredging work in Adam’s Bridge / Palk Strait areas since July, 2009.   On 
23.02.2018, with the approval  of CCPA, the Government filed a ffidavit stating that 
considering the socio -economic dis advantages of a lignment No.6, Go I did not want to 
implement the said a lignment but intended to explore an alternative alignment withou t 
affecting / damaging the Adam's Bridge / Ram Sethu in the interest of the nation.   The 
Hon'ble Apex Court w as requested to dispose of the p etitions accordingly. The matter is sub 
judice since then  and there has been no further n otice from the said Court nor was any 
affidavit filed by the Government.  The recommendations of the Standing Committee have 
been noted.

DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF LIGHTHOUSES AND LIGHT SHIPS  
Recommendation/Observation  
13. The Committee underlines the role of lighthouses and lightships in terms of indication 
of dangerous shoals, sandbanks, rocks etc. to obtain a Line of Position and to indicate 
Landfalls, Headlands, entrance to estuaries/ Ports etc. The Committee notes from the 
information made available to it that the fundin g pattern of the Directorate General of 
Lighthouses and Lightships is based on cost recovery system and that the Directorate does 
not burden the taxpayers as all expenditure on management and development is met out of 
the revenue collected by levy of light  dues. The Committee desires to be apprised of the tariff 
setting mechanism in the Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships/ Ministry.  
                       (Para 82) 
Reply of the Ministry 

12 
 
13.1. The tariff of Lightdues is prescribed by the DGLL considering the operation cost and 
cost of new establishment of Aids to Navigation (AtoN). The present rate of lightdues are as 
follows: 
i) Rs.8.00 /NRT for ships other than container ships 
ii) Rs.92.00 per TEU for container ships. 
13.2. The lightdues are collected only from foreign going ships. Coastal ships/ Home trade

PERFORMANCE OF PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee observes that the parameters of Average Turn -around time and 
Average Output Per Ship Berthday  are not much in vogue in international Ports in terms of 
international best practices. One such parameter widely used internationally is “average 
moves per crane hour”. With the advent of full scale containerization of general cargo, Ports 
have witnessed paradigm shift in terms of commissioning of container terminals. The 
Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to apply the yardstick of “Average moves per 
crane per hour” to measure the performance of the Major Ports. The Committee desires to be 
kept apprised in this regard.          (Para 36) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1. The Port p erformance cannot be assessed based on a single measure. A meaningful 
evaluation of a Port’s performance will require sets of measures relating to the duration of the 
ship’s s tay in port (t otal Turnaround Time in Port), the quality of the cargo handling 
mechanism and the quality of service to inland transport vehicles during their passage 
through the port. 
7.2. The average moves per crane hour are one of the yardsticks for meas uring crane’s 
ability to move the number of containers in an hour.  It is more suitable for Container 
handling ports. Whereas, the majority of Indian Major Ports are multi -commodity Ports 
handling around 75 -80% cargo comprising Liquid Bulk, Dry Bulk, Break -Bulk, etc.  The 
level of containerization in India is increasing but still below the level of leading international 
container handling Ports.   Some of the Major Ports like Kolkata, Haldia, Paradip, New 
Mangalore, Mormugao, Mumbai, etc. do not have a dedicated state -of-art container terminal 
at present.

 16. The Committee takes note of the fact that the East Coast Canal in the Balasore 
district of Odisha has been declared as the NW-5 and the vast agricultural land on both sides 
of the canal depends on the drainage of water during heavy rain in the rainy season. During 
summer season, rabi crops used to be irrigated from this canal. Further, it notes that d ue to 
negligence of authorities, growth of wild shrubs and grass makes the little water available, 
poisonous and it dysfunctions the lift irrigation pumps during summers. They also act as a

signing of the Concession Agreement. Two important ‘Conditions Precedent’ to 
be met by the Concessionaire are furnishing of performance guarantee for 
implementing the project and achievement of financial closure. 
(iv) Independent Engineer to be appointed by the Concessioning Authority in 
consultation with the Concessionaire for approving and monitoring design, 
engineering and construction standards for the Project and to issue Comple tion 
Certificate. Change of scope of the project, if initiated by Port, is allowed at the 
cost of the Concessioning Authority during the construction phase. 
(v) Rights and obligations and risk allocation of both the Concessionaire and 
Concessioning Authority t owards operations and maintenance of the Project 
Facilities and providing supporting infrastructure have been spelt out. Commercial 
operation commences on issue of Completion Certificate. 
(vi) User charges, collected by the Concessionaire are regulated by the T ariff 
Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) or such other Competent Authority under the 
Applicable Laws. 
(vii) As consideration for the Concession awarded, the Concessionaire pays to the 
Concessioning Authority License fee towards project site, equipments and other 
assets /utilities taken over from the Concessioning Authority and a share of gross 
revenue earned from the operation of the project as ‘Royalty’. 
(viii) Provisions have been made for remedial measures to be put in place in case of any 
material adverse effect on account of change in law. 
(ix) Provisions made for (a) premature termination of the Concession Agreement in 
the event of a default in meeting the obligations by either Party, after following 
due consultation process & issue of Termination Notice; and (b) for paym ent of 
compensation on such premature termination arrived as per prescribed basis. 
(x) Dispute Resolution Mechanism under the Arbitration Act, 1996 was prescribed. 
(xi) Procedure to be followed for transfer of project site and assets and equipment 
back to the Conce ssioning Authority by the Concessionaire on expiry of the 
concession period, either by premature termination or by efflux of time was laid 
down. 
6.4. Though Public Private Partnership (PPP) mode had been largely successful in Port 
sector, some PPP projects  experienced difficulties during operations, which necessitated a 
review of the MCA, 2008. 

38 
 
6.5. Keeping in view the recommendations of the Committee constituted in February, 
2010, headed by Shri B.K. Chaturvedi , Member (Planning Commission) with Secretary 
(Ministry of Shipping), Finance Secretary, Secretary (Expenditure) and Joint Secretary 
(PMO) as members; Working group; Committee on revising and revitalising PPP model of 
infrastructure (Kelkar Committee); and the experiences gained in managing PPP projects, the 
MCA, 2008 was amended with a view to obviate the problems being faced in execution of 
PPP Projects on account of certain provisions of the present MCA, in order to enhance 
confidence of investors and ma ke the investments in the Port Sector attractive. The salient 
features of the revised MCA, 2018 are as under:- 
(i) Change in equity holding requirements to provide exit route to developers. 
(ii) Payment of royalty by private operators to Port on “per MT of cargo ha ndled” 
basis instead of “% of gross revenue”. 
(iii) Provision for additional land. 
(iv) Improved utilization of project assets and higher productivity. 
(v) Amendment in definition of “Change in Law”. 
(vi) Provision for commercial operation before COD. 
(vii) Provision for mitigation measures - constitution of a Board. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
6.6. The Committee is concerned to note that some PPP projects have witnessed time 
overruns and cost escalation due to delay in obtaining statutory/security clearances. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to put in place systemic improvements to overcome 
delay in obtaining necessary clearances. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of 
the action taken in this regard. 
 
TRAFFIC HANDLING AT MAJOR PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee desires to know whether the negative growth of the traffic handled at 
the 6 Ports is a result of competition from Minor Ports due to their growth rates and huge 
capacity addition through private sector. The Committee also desires to be appri sed of the 
remedial measures taken to arrest this trend.                 (Para 34)   
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1. The Major Ports fall under the jurisdiction of a regulator, the Tariff Authority for 
Major Ports (TAMP).  This results in a lack of a level playing field for Major Ports.  Major 
Ports end up losing business opportunities due to certain tariff related uncer tainties as 

39 
 
determined by TAMP.  Tariffs at non -Major Ports are not regulated, and they price their 
services based on market and competition. 
7.2. The Government has introduced Major Ports Authority Bill in the Parliament to 
provide greater autonomy to Ports.  The proposed bill aims at decentralizing decision making 
and to infuse a professional approach in governance of Ports.  The Bill is aimed at reorienting 
the governance model in central Ports to the landlord Port model in line with the successful 
global practice.  
7.3. The role of Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) for fixation of the tariff has been 
done away with in the Bill. PPP operators will be free to fix tariffs based on market 
conditions, as notified by the Port Authority. The Board of the Port Authority has been 
delegated the power to fix the scale of rates for other Port services and assets. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.4. The Committee takes cognizance of the fact that the Government has introduced 
the Major Ports Authority Bill in the Parliament which seeks to provide greater 
autonomy to the Major Ports and decentralize decision making. The Committee would 
like the Ministry to pursue vigorously and take the above Bill to its logical conclusion in 
a specified timeframe so that the lack of level playing field for Major Ports is eliminated 
and governance of Major Ports is transformed. The Committee desires to be kept 
updated in this regard.   
 
CONNECTIVITY TO PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation  
8. Lack of rail and road networks has emerged as a major constraint for the Major 
Ports. The Committee observes that connectivity projects are capital intensive and have 
substantial gestation period as they become economically viable over long periods of time. 
The Committee would, therefore, like to know the financial model for implementation of the 
rail-road connectivity projects including sources of their funding and the extent to which 
such models are  viable in India. The Committee is dismayed to note that the Ministry has 
extended timelines for execution of almost three -fourth of the number of projects whereas the 
emphasis should have been on timely and speedy completion of connectivity projects. The 
Ministry should also focus on implementing connectivity projects to link Minor Ports to 
metropolitan cities and State capitals. Processes for all necessary clearances should be 
initiated well in advance to avoid undue bottlenecks and clearance issues.                (Para 44) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1. Majority of rail and road projects are being implemented by Indian Railways, NHAI, 
Major Ports and State Governments with their own funding. While implementation of these 
projects, there is requirement of statutory clearances and land acquisition which usually 
causes delay and project implementation timeline gets extended. Regarding projects 

40 
 
identified under Bharatmala P ariyojana, MoRTH through letter dated 10 th October, 2018, 
intimated that they will execute the projects only when the State Government shall provide 
encumbrance free land, shift the utilities and obtain the necessary statutory clearance like 
environmental clearances for NHAI to issue the tenders for the construction of the road 
project. It may be noted that these conditions are not as per mandate of Bharatmala 
Pariyojana nor was its part of Bharatmala Pariyojana for the execution of road project in 
convergence with Sagarmala Programme. Over and above, letter received from NHAI on 25 th 
February, 2020 stated that the Ministry will frame out the recovery formula/ mechanism for 
both Minor and Major Port road connectivity projects and issue policy guideline in th is 
manner, to which Ministry of Shipping has written to NHAI that they are not in agreement to 
frame such policy and NHAI should implement these projects as per cabinet approval. Efforts 
are on to expedite clearances. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
8.2. The Committee notes from the reply that  there is difference of opinion between 
the Ministry of Shipping and Ministry of Road Transport and Highways/ NHAI 
regarding fulfillment of certain prescribed conditionalities for execution of connectivity 
projects by NHAI. This does not augur well for speedy execution of these projects. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Inter -Ministerial wrangling should be 
resolved expeditiously at the highest level of Government which should define and spell 
out the future course of action with respect to sanctioned connectivity projects to Ports 
so that there is no disconnect between the Ministries concerned. Th e Committee desires 
to be kept apprised of the tangible action taken in this regard. 
8.3. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should formulate proper 
guidelines and conduct a n environmental impact assessment before releasing funds for 
any sanct ioned/ stalled/ ongoing project . Therefore, the Ministry of Shipping should 
work in close coordination with Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, NHAI and 
MoEF&CC to address the delay in projects due to land acquisition and environmental 
clearances. 
Recommendation/Observation  
9. Taking cognizance of the fact that a number of projects for widening and upgrading 
the roads and interlinking them are under implementation, the Committee recommends that a 
dedicated monitoring mechanism be put in place to ensure completion of these projects 
within the approved cost and designated timeline. The Committee desires to be kept apprised 
of the measures taken in this regard.           (Para 48) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1. Regarding implementation of projects related to widening and upgrading roads,

requirements. Ministry monitors those projects with MIS tool developed for Sagarmal a 

41 
 
Programme wherein, implementing agencies provide regular updates for all running projects.

Further Recommendation/ Observation 
9.2. The Committee feels that the identification of critical projects near Major and 
Minor Ports must also envision the related urbanization and environmental issues of its

SHIP BUILDING INDUSTRY 
Recommendation/Observation  
12. The Committee finds that the shipbuilding industry is facing certain financial and 
infrastructural bottlenecks which tend to push back the progress of Shipping industry. India 
has meager contribution of 1 percent in terms of its share in global shipbuildin g sector. In a 
bid to give major push to shipbuilding industry, the Government has unleashed a slew of 
initiatives like formulation of Financial Assistance Policy on shipbuilding in 2015, provisions 
of Government departments including Central Public Sector  Undertakings giving right of 
first refusal to Indian shipyards while procuring or repairing vessels for Governmental or its 
own use and grant of infrastructure status to Indian shipbuilding industry. Smaller countries 
like Vietnam and Philippines are ahea d of India in terms of shipbuilding. The Committee 
observes that a vibrant shipbuilding industry contributes to national GDP by way of 
employment generation and creation of business opportunities and shipbuilding and 
therefore, can contribute immensely to the vision of making India a 5 Trillion Dollar 
economy. It is, therefore, imperative for the Government to encourage the indigenous 
shipbuilding ecosystem. The Committee is also of the opinion that shipbuilding is a capital 
intensive infrastructure industry and therefore, PPP is the way forward. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry must revisit its strategies to enhance the country’s global 
competitiveness in manufacturing of warships and also to build ship equipments for 
Merchant Shipping.                        (Para 70) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1. Ministry has taken various steps to encourage the indigenous shipbuilding ecosystem 
such as: 

43 
 
(i) Grant of financial assistance to shipyards 
(ii) ROFR policy which gives right of first refusal to Indian shipyards with regard to 
shipbuilding orders of Government and PSU for procurement of vessels for their 
own use or government use. 
(iii) Infrastructure status has been provided to shipyards to avail cheap loans and 
working capital. 
(iv) Ministry is considering setting up of a Maritime Development fund to cater to the 
fund requirements of ship building and shipping sector in consultation with World 
Bank. It is expected that with the setting up of Maritime Development fund, the 
indigenous ship building industry would be come globally competitive. An 
ancillary unit has been set up by Cochin Shipyard Limited. It is expected that this 
would help to enhance the capacity and capability for manufacturing ship 
equipment for Merchant Shipping. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
12.2. The Committee appreciates various steps the Ministry has taken to promote 
indigenous shipbuilding ecosystem in t he country. The Committee would however like 
to be apprised of the efficacy of measures initiated.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
  
ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2020-21 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1. The Committee notes that due to broad budgetary cuts imposed by the Ministry of 
Finance, the Ministry has witnessed a reduction in allocation of funds for the Financial Year 
2020-21 and has been allocated only Rs. 2499.83 crore as against its projected dem and of 
Rs. 2647.25 crore.             (Para 23) 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
  
1.1. Factual Statement. Noted by the Ministry. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
2. The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that the difference in the 
projection made by it and the allocation given for the financial year 2020 -21 is not high and 
that if additional funds are required, it would move the Ministry of Finance for add itional 
allocation at the RE 2020 -21 stage.  The Committee observes that availability of adequate 
resources to the tourism sector is sine qua non for achieving the tourism growth as well as 
inclusive growth.  Since development of tourism infrastructure is capital intensive, the 
Committee apprehends that with the budgetary allocation of Rs.2499.83 crore for 2020 -21, 
which, in the opinion of the Committee, is low, it would be difficult for the Ministry to take up 
significant activities related to on-going infrastructure development of the sanctioned tourism 
circuits/destinations and also development of new tourism products of global standards.  If 
the tourism sector has to play a major role in faster and inclusive growth, the infrastructure 
bottlenecks need to be unleashed.  The Committee notes that more than half of the allocation 
of the Ministry for 2020-21 is devoted for the schemes relating to infrastructure development.  
In most of the States/UTs, the outlay for tourism is meagre and the Central Government  has 
dominance in the domain of public resource mobilization by way of collection of tax revenue. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry be provided a higher financial outlay at the RE 
2020-21 stage.  The Committee would like the Ministry of Tourism to  bring the above 
recommendation to the notice of Ministry of Finance and also intimate the Committee of their 
response in this regard.             (Para 27) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1. Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.   The 
recommendations of the Committee have been conveyed to the Ministry of Finance for 

3 
 
necessary action  vide Ministry of Tourism ref . No. G -20017(5) /2019-20 B&A dated 
27.05.2020.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
3. Since the consumption demand arising from tourist expenditure has a multiplier effect 
on the economy, the expansion of the tourist sector can lead to large scale employment 
generation and poverty alleviation. Needless to men tion, tourism has huge potential to 
stimulate overall economic growth and any increase in the outlay for tourism sector can 
propel our country to a faster growth trajectory and will lead to large scale employment 
generation and alleviation of poverty. If o ur country can tap its full potential of the tourism 
sector, it can play a major role for faster and inclusive growth; but for this to happen, the 
budgetary provisions for the Ministry has to be enhanced substantially.  By doing so, tourism 
infrastructure could be strengthened/ upgraded, conservation and development of all 
heritage sites could be undertaken and completed and last mile connectivity to tourist 
destinations could be improved. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government 
should acco rd priority status to the tourism sector and enumerate a fiscal roadmap for 
generating and allocating more financial resource for tourism so that the full potential of a 
vibrant sector could be tapped.          (Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  
3.1. The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.  The   
allocation for the tourism Sector is increa sing year after year.   During the Financial Year 
2020-21, Rs. 2499.83 crores have been allotted  to Ministry of Tourism, which is the highest 
ever allocation of fund made to   the Ministry of Tourism.  The BE allocation during 2018-19 
was Rs. 2150 Crore and during 2019 -20 it was Rs. 2189.22 Crore.    From the BE allocation, 
it is evident that the Ministry of Finance is increasing the budgetary out lay for the flagship 
programmes of this Ministry viz., Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD.  Also, the allocation for 
advertising and publicity to make India a preferred tourist destination is increasing over the 
years.  Further, recommendations of the Committee h ave been conveyed to the Ministry of 
Finance for necessary action.  
  
Recommendation/Observation  
  
4. The Committee notes with dismay the huge mismatch between the projected demand 
for funds and actual allocations made for the Ministry of Tourism for the years 2018 -19 and 
2019-20 as well.  The pattern of shortfall in allocation of funds indicates that budg etary 
requirements are being projected by the Ministry more on the basis of theoretical 
anticipation rather than on actual trend of requirement. The Ministry’s reply that the 
Schemes/Projects undertaken by them are of continuous nature and that the targets  are fixed 
and funds are released as per budgetary allocation by the Ministry of Finance suggests the 
casual and routine manner in which the Budget Estimates are being prepared and the 
Ministry is not very serious about the activities to be undertaken by t hem.  Tourism is 

4 
 
important for both economic growth and employment generation and the corpus of funds 
should not have been arbitrarily decided without reference to any ground reality.     (Para 29) 
  
5. The Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to have the entire requirement of 
funds realistically assessed after collecting timely information on requirement of funds from 
the State Governments and other stakeholders and take steps to rectify and improve upon the 
existing system of assessing requiremen t of funds. The Ministry should formulate 
Schemes/Programmes which can be implemented in a time -bound manner.  The Committee 
desires to be apprised of the specific action taken in this regard.      (Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  
5.1. The projection of demands of funds under the schemes are finalized after assessment 
of  the targets set for the ensuing year with realistic approach, position of the approved 
projects under execution, projects under pipeline and requests for the projects received fr om 
the State Governments/ UTs. Further, these are continuing schemes and any shortfall in funds 
due to re duced allocation at RE stage, can be met from the next year’ s budget. It is also 
submitted that during the preceding four years, all funds allocated under various Schemes 
were successfully utilized.  Further, keeping in view the experience gained and challenges 
faced by the Ministry in operation of various Schemes, scheme guidelines f or various 
schemes are amended as and when required.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
6. The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the Ministry has kept the unspent 
provisions of Rs. 43.18 Crore till the close of the financial year 2018 -19 and surrendered the 
same on 29.03.2019 totally disregarding the provisions of General Financial Rules which 
states that unspent provisions in a grant should be surrendered as soon as they are foreseen, 
without waiting for the last day of the year.  The Committee deprecates such a casual 
approach of the Ministry in adhering to the fiscal discipline and desires the Ministry to avoid 
such lapses in future and surrender unspent budgetary provisions timely so that st arved 
projects/schemes are not deprived of the same.        (Para 31) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  
6.1. The observations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.   The Program 
Divisions of the Ministry have been advised to intimate the amount of savings to Budget & 
Accounts Division of the Ministry well in Advance. 
 
INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF TOURIST CIRCUITS AROUND SPECIFIC 
THEMES (SWADESH DARSHAN) 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
7. The Committee takes note of the remedial measures formulated by the Ministry  for 
effective implementation of the projects sanctioned under the SDS and would like the  

5 
 
Ministry to carry out an appraisal of their efficacy so that the avowed objective of developing 
world class infrastructure in the circuit destinations, promoting cult ural and heritage value 
of the country and providing complete tourism experience with varied thematic circuits under 
the Scheme could be achieved.                    (Para 57) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1. Ministry ensures regular review and monitoring of the sanctioned projects for the 
effective implementation of the Swadesh Darshan Scheme. A detailed last review of all the 
sanctioned projects was undertaken by the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism with all th e States/ 
UTs and Implementing Agencies in January – February, 2020. As a follow -up incessant 
exercise, review meetings were also taken by the Joint Secretary (Tourism) in June, 2020 
with States/ UTs in order to address various issues related to the scheme such as financial and 
physical progress of the projects, UC pendency with the Implementing Agencies, other 
auxiliary issues related to the projects etc. The Ministry of 
Tourism is regularly and aggressively monitoring the progress of the projects at vario us 
levels. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
8. The Committee recommends that for bette r promotion of rural tourism, a cluster 
approach may be pursued rather than a stand -alone approach and more and more Rural 
Circuit Projects may be sanctioned and implemented  for promotion of niche tourism and 
more funds may be earmarked for rural circuits under the SDS.      (Para 60) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1. The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
9. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should pursue with all the State 
Governments the matter of setting up of a State Level Monitoring Committee to remove 
various impediments like delays in land acquisition and statutory clearances so that time 
overrun in Buddhist Circuit Pr ojects is minimized.  This would also speed up execution of 
Buddhist Circuit Projects within the approved cost.        (Para 62) 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1. The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. 
 
DOMESTIC PROMOTION  AND PUBLICITY INCLUDING MARKET  
DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
10.  During his speech from Red Fort last year, Prime Minister Modi  had urged Indians 
to visit at least 15 domestic destinations by the year 2022.  As a part of the Prime Minister's 
vision and in a bid to encourage more footfall on domestic tourist destinations, the Ministry 

6 
 
of Tourism has launched the "Dekho  Apna Desh" campaign.  The Committee notes that there 
have been media reports that the Ministry of Tourism would fund travel expenses of tourists 
who visit 15 tourist destinations in the country under the "Dekho Apna Desh" campaign.  It 
has now been clarified that the  Ministry has no scheme for funding the travel expenses of 
tourists visiting destinations in the country under the "Dekho Apna Desh" campaign.  
However, the Ministry proposes to give recognition to select domestic travellers who 
undertake visits to various  tourist destinations in the country through random selection for 
which details are being finalized.  Apparently, there is lack of policy stance on the incentives 
to be given under the "Dekho Apna Desh" campaign. The Committee expects the Ministry to 
quickly spell out its policy stance on the issue with greater clarity and in unambiguous terms.  
The Committee desires to be apprised in this regard.        (Para 84) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1. Taking the online pledge  by the citizens of the country to travel to 15 destinations in 
the country before 2022 on MyGov platform is one of the main activity under the Dekho 
Apna Desh Campaign. In order to encourage the citizens of  the country to take the said 
pledge, the Ministry of Tourism has decided to give gift hampers in the form of Dekho Apna 
Desh and Incredible India merchandise like T -Shirts, caps, mugs, pen etc. to select people 
who have taken the pledge. The selection of such persons is done peri odically on a   random 
basis through software application.   
 
Recommendation/Observation  
  
11. The Ministry should also provide facilities for Domestic Tourism to sustain the 
growth rate of 11.91%. The Committee desires to be apprised of the precise steps  taken in 
this direction.              (Para 87) 
 
Reply of the Ministry  
11.1. Ministry of Tourism has taken several steps to provide facilities to all tourists 
including domestic tourists as per details given below:- 
  
i. Launched the Swadesh Darshan Scheme with a vision to develop theme based tourist 
circuits. 
ii. Launched the National Mission on Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual, Heritage 
Augmentation Drive (PRASHAD) Scheme for holistic development of identified 
pilgrimage destinations. 
iii. Identified 17 Iconic Sites in the country for development by seeking convergence with 
other Central Ministries/Departments/State Governments /Urban local bodies. 
iv. Launched the Adopt a Heritage Project for development and maintenance of tourist 
amenities at heritage sites/monuments and other tourist sites. 
v. Launched 24x7 toll free multi-lingual tourist helpline. 
vi. Revamped Incredible India website for providing information on tourism 
sites/destinations in different States/ Union Territory Administrations. The 

7 
 
information on  website is available in different international languages including 
Hindi language. 
vii. Lunched Buddhist website – indiathelandofbuddha.in to promote and showcase the 
rich Buddhist Heritage in India. 
viii. Launched Incredible India Tourist Facilitator Certification  Programme, a pan -India 
online learning program. There are two categories of IITF Certification Programme 
i.e., Basic and Advanced (Heritage & Adventure) with an optional specialization 
programme of fluency in spoken foreign language other than English. 
ix. New mountain peaks have been opened for mountaineering/trekking to give boost to 
adventure tourism in the country. 
x. Lowering of G.S.T. on hotels rooms with tariffs of  ₹1,001 to ₹7,500/night to 12% and 
for ₹7,501 & above to 18%. 
  
OVERSEAS PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY INCLUDING MARKET 
DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 
 
Recommendation/Observation   
12. The Committee notes that during 2019 -20, the Ministry had undertaken a number of 
promotional activities under the Overseas Promotion and Marketing  like joint promotions, 
food festivals, organisation of Trade Fairs and Road Shows, Hospitality Programmes, know 
India Seminars for more focused marketing in major and potential source markets, etc.  The 
Committee recommends that the Road Shows focusing on  Niche Tourism Products like 
Adventure Tourism, Medical Tourism, Eco Tourism etc. should also be organised in major 
overseas source markets.                            (Para 101) 
 
Reply of the Ministry  
12.1 The Ministry of Tourism promotes India as a holistic destination at the Road Shows 
held in the tourism generating markets overseas. Focus is also given to the promotion of 
Niche tourism products such as adventure, medical, MICE, cruise etc. In addition, these niche 
tourism segments are also promoted  by the India Tourism Offices overseas at travel 
shows/exhibitions, Know India Seminars, print/electronic/outdoor and online media etc.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
13. The Committee observes that the medium of Cinema is a powerful instrument for 
promotion of tourist destinations.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to 
leverage the medium of cinema for promotion of Indian tourism in overseas markets, the 
Ministry should partner with International Film Festivals world-wide.             (Para 102)  
 
Reply of the Ministry 
 
13.1. The observation is noted and participation would be considered as per merits and 
availability of budget .   Also, the recommendations of the Committee were  brought to the 

8 
 
notice of Ministry of Information & Broadcasting and National Film Development 
Corporation (NFDC) for taking appropriate action at their end. 
 
13.2. NFDC has now stated that  Ministry of Tourism can be integrated with NFDC in 
its two important verticals i.e., Film F acilitation Office (FFO) and NFDC Film Bazaar in 
following areas:-  
a.  Indian tourism can be promoted at key  international film festivals and markets in 
India and abroad such as Marche Du Film (Cannes Film Market), European Film Market in 
Berlin, Hong Kong Film Market (FILMMART),  Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), 
IFFI, Film Bazaar, under the Ministry of Tourism's  brand "Incredible India". This  integrated 
with the Ministry of  I&B’s “Film in India” campaign  would enhance the reach of India as a 
filming destination amongst the global film industry, leading to greater film tourism. An 
integrated multi -media publicity and advertising campaign can give fillip to India’s 
positioning as a preferred filming destination. 
b.  The Ministry of Tourism can support the creation and deve lopment of a location 
database which will specifically highlight and showcase the top end cinematic locations 
across India for filmmakers. The database so created m ay be showcased on the FFO web

Recommendation/Observation  
  
18. Cruise Tourism is a supply -driven market and cruise lines are always in search of 
new markets and destinations.  India’s enchanting and exotic destinations could catapult 
India as one of the leading cruise destinations.  But for that to happen, stable and consistent 
operating conditions will have to be concretized because cruise line companies which 
typically plan two to three years ahead, need to know that the basic conditions of operating 
are stable and consistent.  The Committee, therefore, recommends th at the Ministry of 
Tourism in collaboration with Ministry of Shipping should expedite appropriate policy 
measures for developing India’s largely untapped and hitherto small cruise market and pull 
cruise vessels to its shores.  The Committee desires to be u pdated on the progress made in 
this regard.                   (Para 133) 
Reply of the Ministry 
18.1. This Ministry  brought to the notice of Ministry of Shipping about the 
recommendations of the Committee. The reply of Ministry of Shipping is as follow:- 
  

12 
 
(a) The following steps have been taken by the Government to promote Cruise Tourism 
in India: 
i. A delegation comprising  Secretary (Shipping), Chairmen of two cruise ports and 
Economic Advisor, Ministry of Tourism had participated in the Sea Trade Cruise 
Global h eld in Miami in April, 2019.   This forum was utilized to create awareness 
about cruise shipping in India and the various steps taken in this sector for ease of 
doing business. 
ii.  Foreign flag vessels carrying passengers had initially been allowed to call at Indian 
Ports till 5 th February, 2024 without obtaining a licence from Director General of 
Shipping.  This facility has been extended for a further period of 5 years till 
5th February, 2029. 
iii. Standardized Operating Procedures (SOPs) for cruise vessels have b een revised and 
operationalised w.e.f. November, 2017 at all Major Ports. Thereafter a Monitoring 
Committee for implementation of the SOPs was formulated comprising officials from 
Ministry of Shipping, Ministry of Tourism and CISF. 
iv. To address the manpower, coordination and logistic issues, for handling cruise vessels 
at Ports, Port Level Committees with Chairman of respective Major Ports Trust with 
Secretary Tourism of concerned State as Vice -Chairman and Regional Directors of 
respective regions as conveners have been Constituted by Ministry of Tourism. 
v. E-visa facility has been extended to five sea Major Ports namely Mumbai, Goa, 
Mangalore, Cochin and Chennai. Immigration counters have been set up at the 
aforesaid five Major Ports visited by cruise ships.  
vi. To make India attractive to Cruise passengers and to promote cruise tourism in the 
country, Ministry of Home Affairs has at the request of Ministry of Shipping, 
exempted cruise tourists arriving with e -visa from the requirement of biometric 
enrolment for a period of three years i.e. till 31.12.2020 vide their order   20th 
December, 2017.  This will facilitate in expeditious immigration clearance of cruise 
passengers with e-Visa   enabling them to spend more time on shore. 
vii.  The port charges have been reduced a nd all Major Ports are to charge a uniform 
single rate of $0.35 per GRT for first 12 hrs of stay.   Ports will not charge any other 
rate like berth hire, Port dues, pilotage, passenger fee etc from cruise liners.   The 
above rate has been made effective from 3rd November, 2017 and will remain in force 
for a period of three years. 
viii. Concession of 40% on composite port charges of USD 0.35 per GT for 1st 12 hours 
of stay is given to domestic cruise vessels for 75 -100 calls in a year and 50% 
concession for calls ex ceeding 100 in a year for a period of three years i.e. up to 
3.11.2020 (coinciding with validity of composite Port Charges order) at all Major 
Ports except Mumbai  Port, where concession of 20% for 100 calls or more in a year 

13 
 
(1st October to 30 th September) will be applicable. Further extension of this 
rationalisation of tariff for few more years is also being considered and processed. 
ix. The Ports do not levy any priority/ousting/shifting charges for berthing the cruise 
vessel.  
x. Walk-in berthing/ preferential berthing to home port cruises without any extra charge. 
xi. To address manpower, coordination and logistic issues for handling cruise vessels at 
ports, Port Level Committees with chairman of the respective Major Port Trust as 
Chairman, Secretary Tourism of the concerned state as Vice -Chairman and Regional 
Director of the respective region of Ministry of Tourism as Convener have been 
constituted. 
xii. Immigration counters have been set up at five Major Ports visited by cruise ships.   
(b)  In addition, the M inistry has taken up the following tax related issues with the 
Ministry of Finance: 
i. Customs duty exemption on consumption of goods and services on international 
cruise ships when they are in Indian waters and travel from one port to another port to 
ensure a competitive position of India globally and ease of doing business for cruise 
operations in the country. 
ii. Sale of the cruise tickets/ packages attract s GST at a rate of 18% while sale of airline 
ticket attracts GST of 5% for economy class and 12% for other  classes.  On the 
similar lines, the travel by cruise ships is charged at 5% rate for travel in a 
single/double room cabin and 12% for travel by suites. 
iii. The IGST should be exempted on import of cruise vessels in India.   In pre -GST 
regime cruise ships were exempted from customs duty. 
iv. GST may be exempted for goods supplied on board at home Ports for cruise lines to 
promote making Indian ports as home Ports.To stimulate Indians to purchase tickets 
domestically and to retain the profits in India, it is suggeste d that GST on sale of 
international tickets by domestic sale agents be also exempted.

14 
 
19.1. This Ministry brought to the notice of Inland Waterways Authority of India, Ministry 
of Shipping the recommendations of the Committee.   The reply of Inland Waterways 
Authority of India (IWAI) is as follow:- 
(i)        The IWAI Act, 1985, Section I envisages Inland Waterways Authority of India 
(IWAI) is to develop and regulate National Waterways for cargo shipping and 
navigation and thus development of river cruise tourism is not mandated with IWAI. 
However, the infrastructure developed for transportation on National Waterways by 
IWAI include fairway , terminals, jetties, navigation aids etc. They are used by the 
river cruise tourism operators who are from private sector. IWAI’s role is technical 
facilitator. 
(ii)         River cruise tourism has been a regular feature on National Waterway (NW) -
1(Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system) and NW -2 (river Brahmaputra) since 
several years. Various cruise operators viz., M/s Heritage River Cruises Pvt. Ltd., M/s 
Vivada Inland Waterways and M/s Assam Bengal Navigation Company operate their 
cruise vessels on NW-1, NW-2 and Sunderbans waterways. 
(iii)National Waterway (NW) -1 (Ganga - Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system from 
Allahabad to Haldia), NW – 2 (River Brahmaputra from Dhubri to Sadiya), NW -3 
(West Coast Canal from Kottapuram to Kollam along with Udyogmandal and 
Champakara Canals) have already been developed with fairway navigational aids, 
jetties and terminals with mechanized equipment handling facilities for loading and 
unloading of cargo. 
(iv) In addition to NW -1 & NW -2, NW -3 in Kerala is also a world renowned touris t 
destination for domestic and foreign tourists where house boat tourism with food and 
accommodation facilities are available. The area of operation of these boats includes 
Vembanad lake of Alapuzha, Kuttanad area and Ashtamudi lake of Kollam area in 
NW-3. 
(v)            IWAI under Ministry of Shipping provides navigational channel & assists in 
embarking/ disembarking facility to operators/ passengers. IWAI has 
engaged WAPCOS Limited for preparation of an action plan & detailed road map for 
development of river cruise tourism in India. 
19.2. In a recent initiative, sanction order of Rs 2803.05 lakh dated 19.12.2019 under the 
scheme ‘Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development” has been 
issued by ID -Division, Ministry of Tourism for deve lopment of nine main points of 
embarkation/disembarkation of river cruise on National Waterways 1 and 2 proposed to be 
executed through IWAI by March, 2021.  The tender for assignment of job is under process, 
design of jetties and amenities to be constructe d on shore has been finalised, and the

Recommendation/Observation  
 
1. The Committee takes note of the fact that the annual growth rate of the Tourism 
Sector in India is 5.2% and its contribution to GDP is 5.06%. According to UN World 
Tourism Organisation Report (2011), for diversified economies, the contribution of tourism 
to national GDP is over 10% for countries where tourism happe ns to be the main driver of 
national economy. Quite apparently, despite having a strong domestic tourist base which is 
likely to grow further on the back of a rapidly rising middle class with increased disposable 
incomes and having many World Heritage sites and rich fauna, our country has not been able 
to exploit its tourism potential to the fullest possible extent and the tourist sector has not 
proved to be the proverbial engine of growth for our economy. For a country of our size, with 
wealth of attractions and experiences, this underperformance represents significant foregone 
economic value. Since tourism in the country has the potential to emerge as a key economic 
driver through economic growth and employment generation, the country can make a giant 
leap towards achieving 5 trillion dollar economy by tapping the enormous potential of the 
tourism sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the strategies adopted for 
promotion and development of the tourist sector should be recalibrated to harness the  full 
potential of Indian tourism and double the current contribution of tourism to GDP in the next 
5 years. The Committee would like the Ministry to prepare a vision document, chalking out a 
road map for accelerating the expansion of the tourism sector an d helping achieve a 5 
trillion dollar economy by 2025 by way of a substantial contribution from the tourism sector. 
The Committee, therefore, desires that policy measures may be initiated by the Ministry to 
accelerate the growth momentum of the tourism sec tor and raise the contribution of tourism 
from the current 5.06% to 10% of GDP.         (Para 32) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  
1.1. Tourism is a rapidly evolving industry that has become increasingly competitive in 
the global arena. It is gaining universal acce ptance as an engine of economic growth and has 
forward and backward linkages with other sectors and ability to create more employment 
opportunities for the disadvantaged sections of the society. In order to realize the full 
potential of the tourism sector,  Ministry of Tourism formulates policies for infrastructure 
development, product development, human resource development, publicity & promotion, 
regulation, research, analysis, monitoring and evaluation, etc. State Governments and the 
private sector act as  the main spring of activities and provide the necessary dynamism and 
speed for implementation of these policies/ schemes to enable the growth and development of 
tourism sector in India.

Recommendation/Observation  
 
2. The Committee observes that tourism being a labour -intensive multi-sectoral activity 
characterised by multiple services and industries is a key driver of socio -economic progress 
as well as employment generation and economic development.  The tourism sector has the 
potential to stimulate other economic sectors through its backward  and forward linkages and 
cross-sectoral synergies with sectors like agriculture, handicrafts, transport, construction, to 
name a few.  It is thus evident that any higher investment made in the tourism sector can lead 
to large sale employment generation, a lleviate poverty and propel India to a faster growth 
trajectory.               (Para 25) 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
  
2.1. Factual Statement. Noted by the Ministry. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
 

44 
 
2.2. While recommending higher investment in the tourism sector, the Committee 
had expected the Ministry to formulate appropriate policy measures for spurring up 
higher investment in the tourism sector. This recommendation assumes added 
significance in view of the fact that the growth momentum in the tourism sector has 
witnessed a huge slump in the wake of the lockdown induced by the Covid-19 pandemic, 
causing significant disruptions in the Indian economy. The reply of the Ministry fails  to 
address the core concern of the Committee. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the 
Ministry to quickly formulate an appropriate policy for getting more investments in the 
tourism sector so that the growth momentum in this vital sector could be revived. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
  
3. The Committee is dismayed to note that despite its unique endowments of biodiversity 
and its rich culture and heritage, India’s total share in global international tourist arrivals 
remains a modest 1.24% against the target of 3% while, as per the Report of the Working 
Group of Tourism of the 12 th Five Year Plan, in about 150 countries of the world, tourism is 
one of the 5 top export earners and number one export earner in about 60 countries. When 
measured by the yardstick of its vast tourism resources, India’s low share of tourism arrivals 
is certainly below its potential.  Similarly, the contribution (direct and indirect) of tourism in 
the GDP and the total jobs in the country is estimated to be 5.06% and 12.75% respe ctively, 
which, in the considered opinion of the Committee, is inadequate and way below the massive 
potential that exists. The Committee wishes to point out that in many smaller and developing 
countries, the entire economy of the country depends on tourism  for its survival and tourism 
remains a major source of foreign exchange earnings. That being the case, the world's 
second largest country in terms of population, seventh largest by area, having 7500 km of 
coastline and one of the most endowed regions of t he world in terms of its tourism 
attractiveness, India receives less international tourists than its full potential.  Taking all 
these factors into account, the Committee apprehends that the shortfall of Rs. 147.42 crore in 
BE 2020-21 against the projected  demand of Rs. 2647.25 crore would seriously jeopardize 
the targeted tourism outcomes during the Financial Year 2020-21.          (Para 26) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1. The   allocation of Rs. 2499.83 crores  during the Financial Year 2020 -21 is the

insufficient, additional allocation would be projected to the Ministry of Finance at that 
stage.    
Further Recommendation/ Observation

Committee and arriving at empirically correct impact of the shortfall, the action taken 

45 
 
note only highlights projection of additional allocation at the RE stage, if the need so

entire gamut of issues on the targeted tourism outcomes due to shortfall of Rs 1 47.42

8.  The Committee notes that the PRASHAD has been launched with the objective of 
holistic development of identified pilgrimage and heritage destinations and aims at 
infrastructure development.  Since the provision of infrastructure is a prerequisite towards

suggestive of laxity in the monitoring system of the Ministry and the Sta te Governments. This

Recommendation/Observation  
9. The Committee notes that the Scheme of Domestic Promotion and Publicity including 
Market Development Assistance was launched with the major objective of creating a general 
awareness amongst the domestic population about the tourist destinations and to deve lop 
tourist market within the country. The Committee observes that it is often seen that the 
researches pertaining to travel and tourism take place mainly on inbound and outbound 
tourist numbers and Domestic Tourism is given lesser importance. But, since d omestic 

51 
 
tourism generates income redistribution effect from tourists to local population and is also a 
catalyst for various other multiplier effects throughout the value chain, boosting local 
economy as well as national economy in the process, it should no t be regarded as opposed or 
an alternative to Overseas Tourism. Instead these two forms of tourism should complement 
each other. The Committee, therefore, recommends that statistical data should be collected

various types of domestic tourism statistics should be addressed.            (Para 85)

9.1. Our tourism economy is highly dependent on the domestic tourism. Ministry of

9.2. The Scheme of Domestic Promotion and Publicity including Hospitality  (DPPH) of 
Ministry of Tourism is created with the objectives of increasing awareness about tourism 
destinations and products, promoting tourism within the country with focus on priority areas

Recommendation/Observation  
  
10. The Committee observes that there is significant potential for the tourist sector in 
India to generate jobs and absorb a substantially higher workforce.  However, India faces 
intense shortage of trained manpower at various levels of the tourist sector.  It is in this 
context that creating appropriate employable skills in the population assumes added 
significance.  The Committee is, therefore, constrained to note that there is huge variation 
between the annual target fixed and the actual achievement made in the matter of training 
and certification as the Ministry has been able to train/certify a total of 38,859 persons only 
under the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service Providers against its annual target of 
1,01,900 persons during the year 2018 -19. The Committee desires to know the reasons for 
the same. Similarly, the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service Providers could not achieve 
its targets during 2019 -20 as well.  Obviously, there are serious shortcomings in the 
implementation of the training pro grammes under CBSP.  This calls for serious 
introspection.  The Committee desires to be apprised of the remedial measures taken to 
overcome the shortcomings and achieve the intended targets.                (Para 119)

with previous two rounds. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of 
Tourism, in coordination with the Ministry of Civil Aviation, and through the Inter -

operationalisation of these 36 tourist routes/sectors.  The Committee would like to be 
apprised of the progress made in this regard.                 (Para 146)

Recommendation/Observation  
16. The Committee observes that safety and security of tourists is of vital importance as 
any adverse impression in this regard has serious implications on tourist arrivals to the 
country.  In the past, there have been numerous incidents of crime reported agai nst foreign 
tourists in some popular destinations across the country.  In order to make India a safe 
tourist destination where tourists would feel safe and feel free to move around, the State 
Governments/ UT Administrations of Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Karnatak a, Kerala, 
Maharashtra, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Punjab, 
Rajasthan, Sikkim and Uttar Pradesh have set up tourist police in one form or the other.  The

committed and professionally trained tourist police should be deployed at all important 
destinations of tourist importance so that foreign and domestic tourists visiting tourist 
destinations are assured of their safety and security.  The Committee would, therefore, like 
the Ministry of Tourism to take up the matter up with the remaining States/UTs at the highest

ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2020-21 
 The emphasis made  by the Committee in Para 24 of its 275 th Report was on 
highlighting the huge variations in the Budget Estimates and Revised Estimates which 
was indicative of the shortcoming in the budgetary planning. The Committee would, 
therefore, like the Ministry to t ake corrective steps to arrest such an erratic projection 
of requirement of funds and ensure realistic formulation of Budget Estimates. 
                  (Para: 1.2)  
While recommending higher investment in the tourism sector, the Committee 
had expected th e Ministry to formulate appropriate policy measures for spurring up 
higher investment in the tourism sector. This recommendation assumes added 
significance in view of the fact that the growth momentum in the tourism sector has 
witnessed a huge slump in the wake of the lockdown induced by the Covid-19 pandemic, 
causing significant disruptions in the Indian economy. The reply of the Ministry fails to 
address the core concern of the Committee. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the 
Ministry to quickly formulate an appropriate policy for getting more investments in the 
tourism sector so that the growth momentum in this vital sector could be revived.   
                  (Para: 2.2) 
 
The Committee had pointed out an adverse impact of the shortfall of Rs. 147.42 
crores on the targeted tourism outcomes. Instead of addressing this core concern of the 
Committee and arriving at empirically correct impact of the shortfall, the action taken 
note only highlights projection of additional allocation at the RE stage, if the  need so 
arises. The Committee, therefore, expects a factual note to be furnished detailing the 
entire gamut of issues on the targeted tourism outcomes due to shortfall of Rs 147.42 
crores in BE allocation.           
                  (Para: 3.2) 
 
The Comm ittee notes that the Ministry, in its Action Taken Note, has simply 
shared the steps taken to liquidate pending UCs; but skipped to mention about a 
dedicated mechanism to resolve the issue of pending UCs within a specified timeline. 
The Committee deprecate s the Ministry for choosing to remain silent on the issue and 
desires to be kept apprised of the mechanism evolved for addressing the recurring 
problem of pending UCs within a given time-frame.       
                  (Para: 4.3)

 The Committee takes note of the measures in place to monitor the progress of 
implementation of projects under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme. The Committee would, 
however, recommend that a web -based monitoring system/ online portal should also be 
developed to monitor the progress level of the projects sanctioned under the SDS and it 
should also have a feature of uploading photos/ videos made by the Project Monitoring 
Committee during its visit to th e project site. This would ensure greater transparency 
and accountability.          (Para: 5.2)  
The Committee is constrained to note that against an amount of Rs. 627.40 
crores approved in December, 2019 for the 10 projects sanctioned under the Rural 
Circuit during 2018 -19, only Rs. 45.01 crores has been released so far which indicates 
that the Ministry has not exercised due diligence in its Budget formulation which may 
result in massive financial underperformance under this Head. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should urgently address the pending issues 
pertaining to the implementation of the 10 projects and ensure their implementation in 
right earnest so that scarce resources are not kept locked up.           
                  (Para: 6.2) 
The Committee is constrained to note that there has been substantial under -
utilization of funds released against four out of the five projects under the scheme of 
Development of Buddhist Circuit. In a country like ours, where resources are sca rce, 
under-utilization of nearly 50% of allocation is a matter of great concern. The 
Committee would, therefore, recommend that the Ministry should atleast now take 
appropriate corrective measures to address the factors which have led to the financial 
underperformance and time overruns.               (Para: 7.4)
